What's tested
  • The major glands and their hormones, and the three hormone classes with an example of each ("you'll need to know that there's 3 main types of hormones")
  • The oral findings of each disorder: acromegaly's growing jaw, hyper- and hypothyroidism, hyper- and hypoparathyroidism on the radiograph, Addison disease, Cushing syndrome, diabetes, and puberty, pregnancy and menopause
  • His clinical points: implants wait until growth stops, the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery, epinephrine in hyperthyroidism, extra steroid after a big procedure in Addison disease
  • The diabetic patient: his numbers (HbA1c above 7 is poorly controlled; a glucose under 60 needs sugar), the checks before treatment and the rescue for hypoglycemia: finger-stick, glucose rather than table sugar, glucagon if that fails
  • Recognizing three emergencies: thyroid storm (call 911), adrenal crisis and hypoglycemia
  • His three cases, which he walked through by asking the class: Graves disease, a type 2 diabetic who needs an extraction (and his pack-year question), and Addison disease with oral pigmentation

Dr. Chad Taylor (DMD, BSN) gave Lecture A on Friday, November 6, at 8 am. His deck, "Endocrine System Review", makes a fast pass through each gland, shows what its disorders look like in the mouth and how they change treatment, and ends with three patient cases. He added stories from his clinic and his years in surgery and quizzed the class through the cases. These notes follow his recording and his slides. Where he said something that another lecture in this exam teaches differently, the notes say which to use.

His learning objectives: describe the major endocrine glands and hormones; explain how hormones act and are regulated; recognize how endocrine disorders affect oral health and dental treatment; apply endocrine physiology to assessing and managing dental patients; and correlate endocrine dysfunction with common oral findings. Three of the five are about patients, so practice with the cases.

What the endocrine system does

The endocrine system regulates six jobs: growth and development, metabolism, reproduction, stress responses, calcium and phosphate homeostasis, and fluid and electrolyte balance. Every disorder later in the lecture is one of these jobs done too much or too little.

He contrasted it with the nervous system, which does similar work in a different way. Speed of response: the nervous system is always faster, because it works on electrical signals through nerves spread all over the body. The endocrine system releases its hormones into the bloodstream, and the blood takes time to carry them around. Duration of action: hormones act longer, and they also take longer to shut off, so when the endocrine system overreacts, the body takes longer to bring it back under control.

Hormone classes and how they act

"You'll need to know that there's 3 main types of hormones," he said: amines, such as epinephrine and norepinephrine; peptides, such as insulin; and steroids, such as estrogen or testosterone.

Hormones act through cell-surface receptors, often working through second messenger systems, or through intracellular receptors: steroids cross the cell membrane, act at the nucleus and turn on DNA transcription. Peptides such as insulin bind on the cell surface.

Most systems are held in range by negative feedback, much of it in the hypothalamus and pituitary: when a hormone builds up, the brain senses it and turns production down. His example: when testosterone spikes, the pituitary turns down the gonadotropin that drives it (he named FSH; Lectures 13 and 15 teach that LH drives the Leydig cells' testosterone, so use LH if a question asks). Aromatase balances it by converting testosterone to estrogen; a man taking large doses of testosterone, for bodybuilding say, can outrun it, and the imbalance raises his cardiovascular risk.

Keep feedback in mind for Addison disease, because it explains the oral pigmentation: when the adrenal cortex makes too little cortisol, nothing turns ACTH down, so ACTH rises.

The hypothalamus and pituitary

The hypothalamus and pituitary are the control center. The hypothalamus sends releasing and inhibiting hormones to the pituitary, and the anterior pituitary's hormones then drive the other glands: if you need more cortisol, the pituitary releases more ACTH.

HormoneMajor function
ACTHAdrenal cortex stimulation
TSHThyroid stimulation
GH (growth hormone)Growth regulation
FSH and LHReproductive function
ProlactinLactation

Growth hormone stays with you for life, but it is strongest in childhood and adolescence. What stops the long bones from growing is the sex hormones: at puberty the growth plates fuse, and growth hormone no longer lengthens them. He uses this in treatment planning. A 13- or 14-year-old boy who is growing hair on his upper lip is probably close to puberty and near his final height. If a patient lost a tooth at 10, he waits for growth to stop before placing an implant: an implant is fixed in the bone, and if the face is still growing, everything moves around it.

The posterior pituitary has two hormones. ADH conserves water. Too little ADH is diabetes insipidus: the kidneys let out far too much fluid, so the patient is very thirsty all the time. Don't confuse it with diabetes mellitus, the insulin disease: same first word, different hormone. Oxytocin, the "connection hormone" of delivery, is the other. His trivia: alcohol lowers ADH (so you urinate) and nicotine raises it.

Growth hormone excess: acromegaly

Too much growth hormone before puberty, while the long bones are still open, makes a person very tall, 7 feet or more. After puberty the long bones are fused, so they barely grow, and the condition is acromegaly. The hands and feet enlarge, but "look for the jaw in your patients": the mandible grows, so the bite changes, from a normal Class I to edge-to-edge or even a Class III malocclusion. The bigger arch leaves more room for the teeth, so diastemas open between them, and the tongue enlarges (macroglossia). Macroglossia also appears under hypothyroidism, so it is the jaw and the spacing that point to growth hormone.

The thyroid

The thyroid makes T3 and T4, regulated by TSH from the anterior pituitary. They act on metabolism, and the thyroid works like the body's thermostat, so thyroid disease shows in heat intolerance and in weight. That is why the two disorders are mirror images: too much hormone speeds the body up, and too little slows it down.

A surgical point he made from his years in the operating room: the recurrent laryngeal nerve runs through the thyroid area, and the first thing a surgeon does in a thyroidectomy or a parathyroidectomy is find it. Damage to it paralyzes half of the vocal cords, leaving a hoarse, raspy voice that is usually permanent.

Hyperthyroidism is something you will see only on occasion. He said it is generally associated with an adenoma, a tumor of the gland that makes too much hormone. (His own Graves case is the other cause, and Lecture 12a teaches that Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism.) It brings weight loss, tachycardia and heat intolerance. For the dentist: the patient has increased sensitivity to epinephrine, so avoid excessive vasoconstrictor use in uncontrolled disease, since another stimulant raises an already fast heart rate and blood pressure; and in children, accelerated tooth eruption: if permanent teeth come in early, ask the family to have the child's thyroid checked.

Hypothyroidism you will see far more often. It brings fatigue, weight gain and at times bradycardia. It can delay eruption, but what you are more likely to see is macroglossia and delayed wound healing. Most of these patients take thyroid hormone to replace what they lack.

The epinephrine caution belongs to hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism. Statement questions like to move one finding to the other side, so learn this table as pairs: weight lost or gained, a fast or a slow heart, early or late eruption.

Thyroid storm

Thyroid storm, also called thyroid crisis or thyrotoxic crisis, is rare, but it happens: the gland releases a large amount of hormone in a short time. It is a life-threatening emergency. The signs are a high fever, a rapid heart rate, 140 or higher, agitation, anxiety, shakiness, nausea and even delirium. "If you start to see signs and symptoms of this, call 911." In his Graves case, the first thing he would check is the heart rate.

In the chair, thyroid storm can look like hypoglycemia, because both bring a racing pulse, shakiness and confusion. The fever and the high blood pressure point to thyroid storm. Sweating is on his hypoglycemia list, but a hyperthyroid patient sweats too, as the Exam 1 thyroid lecture taught, so it doesn't settle the question.

The parathyroids and calcium

There are four parathyroid glands, and their job is calcium homeostasis. In a parathyroidectomy, he said, surgeons usually leave the patient half of one gland, embedded in a neck muscle, so some tissue keeps managing calcium.

Three hormones keep blood calcium in range.

  • Parathyroid hormone, or PTH, is the fast-acting regulator, under negative feedback. It raises blood calcium three ways. At bone, he said, it inhibits osteoblasts and stimulates osteoclasts, so bone is resorbed. At the kidney, it increases calcium reabsorption. And it has the kidneys release calcitriol, active vitamin D, which makes the GI tract absorb more calcium. His summary: the body takes calcium from the bones, keeps what it already has, and absorbs more.
  • Vitamin D is the long-term regulator. We make it in the skin in an inactive form; the active form comes from the kidney, and it helps the gut absorb calcium.
  • Calcitonin works the other way. Increased blood calcium stimulates the thyroid to release calcitonin, which reverses PTH's effects on bone: "essentially the reverse of parathyroid hormone."

He said "inhibits osteoblasts, stimulates osteoclasts," as on his slide. If a question asks which cell PTH acts on, use Exam 1's mechanism: the PTH receptor is on the osteoblast, which then activates the osteoclasts through RANK ligand; calcitonin acts on the osteoclast itself. Both agree on the result: more osteoclast resorption, more calcium in the blood.

Hyperparathyroidism on the radiograph

Too much PTH means too much bone resorption, and at times osteoporosis. On radiographs, look for loss of the lamina dura. On a normal film, a thin white line outlines the socket: that is the lamina dura, the harder, denser bone the periodontal ligament attaches to. The thin dark line between it and the root is the PDL space. In hyperparathyroidism the white line is lost: the bone looks diffuse and gray right up to the tooth, with no definite outline.

You may also see brown tumors and tooth mobility. A brown tumor shows on a panoramic radiograph as a radiolucent area; his example sat in the bone below a premolar. If you find one, ask the patient about other symptoms and send them to their physician to be checked.

Hypoparathyroidism

Too little PTH means hypocalcemia, and because muscles need calcium to work, low calcium shows as neuromuscular irritability and tetany, muscles that lock up and don't relax. "You need to understand the calcium metabolism side of this, and also its effects on oral and maxillofacial bone."

The adrenal cortex

The cortex makes the two hormones he lists. Cortisol handles the stress response, immune regulation and glucose metabolism. Aldosterone handles sodium retention and potassium regulation. Patients on long-term corticosteroids show cortisol's effects, especially a higher blood glucose and a weaker immune system.

Addison disease is the deficiency. The adrenal cortex fails, and cortisol is the main hormone lacking, often with reduced aldosterone too. Clinically: hypotension, because the kidneys lose salt and the water goes with it, so blood volume falls; fatigue; and hyperpigmentation, brown and black patches on the gums and tongue. The more extensive form is diffuse oral melanosis. If you see these patches, have the patient checked.

Why the pigment? "I didn't really give you guys this," he said, so he told the class: with little cortisol, negative feedback no longer holds ACTH down, so ACTH production increases, and the extra ACTH stimulates melanocytes, darkening the skin and the oral mucosa. It is high ACTH, not cortisol, that colors the mouth.

Adrenal crisis is the emergency of Addison disease. It can be set off by stressful or lengthy surgical procedures, significant infection or trauma, and a missed steroid dose. Any stressful event, an extraction included, normally makes the body produce more corticosteroid, and these patients can't, so after a bigger procedure they may need supplemental corticosteroid, usually a larger dose than normal; agree on the dose with their physician first. The signs of a crisis are severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, loss of consciousness and shock.

Cushing syndrome is the other side: the body makes too much corticosteroid, and the patient looks like someone on long-term steroid therapy. Fat moves to the face and the back of the neck, giving a moon face and a buffalo hump, and there is hyperglycemia. In the mouth, plan for an increased infection risk and delayed healing.

The adrenal medulla

The medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine, the fight-or-flight hormones: the heart speeds up, vessels constrict, the bronchioles dilate and the stomach stops moving. Its dental significance is vasoconstrictor use, the epinephrine in local anesthetics, and stress management during treatment.

His memory tool for cortex versus medulla: a corticosteroid is called that because it comes from the adrenal cortex. The medulla is epinephrine and norepinephrine.

The pancreas

The pancreas makes digestive enzymes too, but his focus is its two opposite hormones. Alpha cells make glucagon, which breaks down glycogen, the sugar stored in the liver and muscles, and drives gluconeogenesis: without food, the body makes its own glucose for the brain from muscle and triglycerides.

Metformin inhibits gluconeogenesis, and he drew a chair-side warning from it. A type 2 diabetic took her medicines but skipped breakfast to make the appointment. She has blocked her own glucose production and eaten nothing, so in his example she is at high risk of hypoglycemia in your chair; be ready with glucose if she turns sweaty or agitated. (Lecture 11 teaches that metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia; insulin and the secretagogues are the usual cause. Either way, ask about the meal.)

Beta cells make insulin, which moves glucose into muscle and fat cells. Excess glucose is stored first as glycogen, which has limited room, then as fat: insulin is the storage hormone.

Diabetes mellitus

Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of the beta cells. It usually starts young, and because the body makes no insulin, these patients need insulin injections to survive. Type 2 diabetes is insulin resistance: the cells' receptors don't respond to insulin, so the pancreas makes more, and these patients have hyperinsulinemia, higher than normal insulin, with a high blood glucose. In type 2 the insulin is ineffective, not deficient. His slides add that production may decline over time.

His numbers for the chair:

MeasureWhat it means
Finger-stick glucose under 60Hypoglycemia: give sugar
Fasting glucose well over 100May have diabetes: insulin isn't clearing the blood
HbA1c about 5 percentTypical for a person without diabetes
HbA1c below 7 (below 6 even better)Generally well controlled

For diagnosis, use Lecture 11's cutoffs: prediabetes is an HbA1c of 5.7 to 6.4 percent or a fasting glucose of 100 to 125, and diabetes is 6.5 percent or 126 and above. He called an HbA1c above 5.3 a sign of risk for prediabetes. His 7 percent is the line for control in a patient who already has diabetes, and it is the number to know for this lecture.

The type 2 drugs he named: metformin; the sulfonylureas, which make the beta cells release more insulin; and newer drugs such as dapagliflozin (Farxiga), which acts on the sodium-glucose transporter in the kidney so the extra sugar is passed in the urine. Sugar in the urine feeds Candida and bacteria, so these patients have a higher risk of urinary tract infections.

The oral manifestations of diabetes are xerostomia (the most common, but not specific), candidiasis, burning mouth syndrome, delayed healing, and an increased risk of periodontal disease and of dental caries. Why the candidiasis and caries: saliva is filtered blood, so a high blood glucose puts more sugar in the saliva, which feeds Candida and Streptococcus mutans.

The periodontal connection is bidirectional. When diabetes worsens, periodontal disease worsens, and periodontal inflammation worsens glycemic control, so keeping their mouths clean, and their home care, matters to their diabetes.

Why does an uncontrolled diabetic heal poorly after an extraction? In class he named high glucose, poor immune function and decreased neutrophil function; his slides add poor blood supply and impaired collagen synthesis. His two dental concerns follow: delayed healing, so be prepared for a long recovery, and an increased risk of postoperative infection.

Two warnings from a patient of his. Some patients wear a continuous glucose monitor, or CGM, a sensor taped to the arm. Some CGMs only read down to a certain level: his patient's stopped at 53, and her finger-stick was in the 30s. It took 10 or 12 packets of glucose gel to bring her back. She also took Mounjaro, and GLP-1 drugs slow the gut, so glucose given by mouth reaches the blood more slowly than you expect.

If oral glucose doesn't work and there is no IV, glucagon can be given intramuscularly or subcutaneously: it breaks down stored glycogen and drives gluconeogenesis, which may also override the metformin. It is a last-ditch option that often isn't on hand: the school's dental clinic doesn't stock it, and at about 480 dollars a dose it is the costliest item in an emergency kit.

Not all sugars are the same. Table sugar, sucrose, is half glucose and half fructose, and the body can't use fructose (or galactose) directly: the liver has to convert it to glucose first. Straight glucose needs less processing, so it raises the blood sugar faster.

Reproductive endocrinology

The sex hormones, estrogen, progesterone and testosterone, are driven by the pituitary, and their oral effects change with the stage of life. Pregnant women tend to have more gingival inflammation because their estrogen and progesterone are higher. Besides pregnancy gingivitis, he sees the pyogenic granuloma, or "pregnancy tumor", fairly often: an overgrowth of gum tissue, usually in the interproximal region. His explanation to patients: the body is on guard, and the gums overreact. At menopause the sex hormones fall, which brings xerostomia, altered taste and effects on bone, possibly osteoporosis.

His case: Lucilla, a racing heart

A 42-year-old woman comes in for a routine cleaning and says her heart feels like it's racing. She was recently diagnosed with Graves disease and takes methimazole. She has lost weight despite a bigger appetite ("a warning bell automatically"), can't tolerate heat, has a tremor and anxiety, and her thyroid gland is enlarged. Her blood pressure is 142 over 88 and her pulse is 112.

His answers: the gland is the thyroid, and the elevated hormones are T3 and T4. Use epinephrine cautiously: she is already overstimulated, and another stimulant could put her at risk. In the mouth: accelerated eruption in younger patients, more caries, burning mouth, and the tremor ("try doing dentistry on a moving object"). The emergency to fear is thyroid storm; the first thing he would check is her heart rate, usually over 140 in a storm.

His case: Proximo, an extraction in an uncontrolled diabetic

A 68-year-old man needs non-restorable mandibular first molars extracted. He has had type 2 diabetes for 22 years, has hypertension, takes his metformin irregularly, reports frequent thirst and urination, and smokes a pack a day. His blood pressure is 148 over 92, pulse 84. In the mouth: generalized moderate periodontal disease, delayed healing of a previous extraction site, dry mouth and multiple carious lesions. His fasting blood glucose is 220 milligrams per deciliter, and his HbA1c is 9.8 percent.

His quick quiz on the smoking: the pack-year history is packs per day times years smoked, so one pack a day for 40 years is 40 pack-years. "Don't forget that. You'll need to know that next year for clinic."

His answers: the organ is the pancreas, and the hormone is insulin, most likely ineffective rather than deficient, because type 2 patients are typically hyperinsulinemic. His periodontal disease is worse because of impaired healing and more food for the bacteria. Before the extraction, be prepared for delayed wound healing, verify his glycemic control and time the procedure after his meal and medication.

His case: Commodus, brown patches in the mouth

A 25-year-old man asks about pigmentation in his mouth. He was diagnosed with Addison disease three years ago and has chronic fatigue, weight loss, dizziness when he stands up, and muscle weakness. The exam shows diffuse brown pigmentation of the buccal mucosa and gingiva, and his blood pressure is 90 over 60.

His answers: the affected gland is the adrenal cortex, not the medulla, which makes epinephrine and norepinephrine. The deficient hormone is cortisol, often with reduced aldosterone, but cortisol is the main worry. The pigment comes from increased ACTH stimulating melanocytes. Surgery, infection or a missed dose could set off an adrenal crisis, and he may need extra corticosteroid after a bigger procedure. In a crisis, expect severe hypotension (his pressure is already low), weakness, confusion and shock.

His deck ends with a "Words of Warning" slide, an image he showed with only "Gentlemen, remember that." Nothing in it is tested.

What's tested
  • hCG: made by the trophoblasts, it rescues the corpus luteum ("this is the important part... this is what rescues the corpus luteum"), keeps progesterone and estrogen high and LH and FSH low, and is what a pregnancy test measures; the corpus luteum carries the first trimester, then the placenta takes over
  • Lactation: prolactin makes the milk and oxytocin lets it down; during pregnancy progesterone holds prolactin back ("what you should know"); dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin, suckling turns it down, and prolactin inhibits GnRH ("one thing that I want to highlight")
  • Fertilization: ZP3 sets off the acrosomal reaction ("one of those proteins that's really important"), then ZP2, the second meiotic division and the cortical reaction that blocks polyspermy; capacitation has to come first
  • The pregnancy steroids ("the main hormones that I care more about"): estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy; the placenta makes progesterone on its own but needs the fetus's 17,20 desmolase to make estrogen
  • Implantation (trophoblasts, cytotrophoblasts versus syncytiotrophoblasts, decidualization) and the placenta's other hormones: human placental lactogen opposes insulin, and relaxin keeps the uterus quiet
  • Labor: a rising estrogen-to-progesterone ratio, prostaglandins and oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which also limits bleeding after delivery; and the endocrine basis of contraception

Dr. Matthew Madison (PhD, Division of Pulmonary, Allergy and Critical Care Medicine) gave Lecture 17 on Tuesday, November 10, at 2 pm, the hour after his lecture on female reproductive physiology. His deck, "Endocrinology of Pregnancy", follows a pregnancy from start to finish: getting sperm and oocyte together, fertilization, implantation and the placenta, the placenta's hormones, delivery, lactation, and a last slide on controlling fertility. He said the emphasis is on the hormones, not on fetal development. These notes follow the recording and slides.

His objectives: describe the events of fertilization; relate the maternal endocrine changes that promote fertilization; relate how the sperm become capable of fertilization; explain how implantation and placentation occur; describe maternal-fetal endocrine communication; and discuss the endocrine basis of contraception.

Why the cycle matters: a quick review

He opened by tying this lecture to the menstrual cycle: pregnancy shows why the cycle has a follicular phase and a luteal phase. In the follicular phase, the first half of the cycle, the growing follicle makes estradiol, and the endometrium is in its proliferative phase, with a lot of cell division. Ovulation comes at midcycle. In the luteal phase, the ruptured follicle turns into the corpus luteum, "a robust endocrine organ," his slide says, that makes large amounts of progesterone, with estrogen. Progesterone is the key hormone that prepares the endometrium for implantation. In the secretory phase, which is the same as the luteal phase, the endometrium's blood vessels become wider and more defined and glycogen vacuoles form. The glycogen is energy for implantation, for building the placenta and for the developing fetus.

Without a pregnancy, the corpus luteum lasts about 14 days after ovulation. Then it regresses into a scar, the corpus albicans; estrogen and progesterone fall abruptly, and the endometrium is shed. Keep that in mind: the first hormone of pregnancy exists to stop it.

His review slide adds three more points. Progesterone raises the basal body temperature, which stays up through the luteal phase. Vaginal cornification, a keratinization driven by estradiol, toughens the vaginal lining so it withstands physical stress. And the cervical mucus decides how easily sperm get through: under estradiol it turns watery and elastic around ovulation, and in the luteal phase it becomes thick.

The road to fertilization

About 250 million sperm are deposited in the vagina, and only about 50 make it to the distal fallopian tube, where fertilization usually happens. Those few are the ones likely to fertilize the oocyte released at ovulation. His slide adds that sperm keep their fertilizing capacity for 24 to 48 hours.

Around ovulation, estrogen dominates, and it helps the sperm survive and move in three ways.

  • It buffers the vaginal pH. He said it raises the pH, making the vagina less acidic, which protects the sperm.
  • It decreases the viscosity of the cervical mucus: a more watery mucus that sperm swim through easily.
  • It increases contraction of the myometrium, the thick muscle layer just under the endometrium. Its rhythmic contractions help propel the sperm up toward the tubes.

On the oocyte's side, the cilia of the fallopian tube help capture the released oocyte and move it down the tube; his slide adds that contraction of the ampulla helps move the egg too.

Three layers around the oocyte

Even the sperm that reach the oocyte face three barriers, from the outside in.

  • The expanded cumulus: the granulosa cells that surround the ovulated oocyte and keep nourishing it. He called this outer layer the corona radiata.
  • The zona pellucida: a specialized extracellular matrix, a thick, rigid capsule around the oocyte.
  • The oocyte's own plasma membrane, the oolemma, which the sperm finally merges with.

Getting through takes the acrosome, the cap on the sperm's head that is packed with enzymes, hyaluronidases and proteases, that break down the zona pellucida. Many sperm working together first break down the cells of the corona radiata.

Histology texts use "corona radiata" for the innermost layer of cumulus cells, the ones touching the zona pellucida. The lecture uses it for the whole cumulus layer. Either way it is the outermost barrier the sperm meets.

Fertilization: ZP3, ZP2 and one sperm per egg

"One of those proteins that's really important is called ZP3." ZP3 sits on the zona pellucida; his slide calls it a species-specific receptor. When a sperm recognizes and binds ZP3, the binding sets off the acrosomal reaction: the acrosome ruptures and releases its enzymes, which digest a path through the zona pellucida. "So ZP3 stimulates the acrosomal reaction."

The acrosome's proteases also cleave the ZP3 layer, so it is shed, and a new layer of proteins is exposed. One of them is ZP2. After the acrosomal reaction, the sperm binds ZP2 instead, because the ZP3 receptors are gone.

Binding ZP2, he said, starts two things.

  • The oocyte undergoes its second meiotic division and becomes haploid, right before fertilization. He asked the class when the first division happened: at ovulation.
  • The cortical reaction, also called the zonal reaction: the oocyte releases its cortical granules, and the remaining zona proteins are shed, so no other sperm can bind. That prevents polyspermy, fertilization by more than one sperm. A single sperm fertilizes a single egg.

Soon after, the male and female pronuclei fuse, and the result is a zygote.

ProteinWhen the sperm binds itWhat the binding starts
ZP3First, on reaching the zona pellucidaThe acrosomal reaction: enzymes digest the zona, and the ZP3 layer is cleaved away
ZP2After the acrosomal reaction, once ZP3 is goneThe oocyte's second meiotic division, and the cortical (zonal) reaction that blocks polyspermy

He and his slide tie the second meiotic division to ZP2 binding. Textbooks such as Costanzo and Guyton say the oocyte completes it once the sperm enters, as it fuses with the oolemma. Both put it at fertilization, right before the pronuclei fuse, which is what to know.

Capacitation: sperm aren't ready on arrival

Ejaculated sperm cannot fertilize an ovum right away. They arrive in a dormant state, and capacitation has to happen first. The reason is a safety lock. While sperm are stored in the male tract, they sit among vesicles rich in cholesterol, which keep adding cholesterol to their plasma membrane. That makes the membrane so rigid that the acrosome can't rupture too early.

In the female tract, the sperm swim away from those vesicles, and the uterine and tubal fluids wash away the inhibitory factors. His slide lists four changes.

  • Membrane fluidity changes as sterols, such as cholesterol, and glycoproteins are removed from the sperm membrane.
  • Proteins and carbohydrates that would block the egg-binding sites are removed.
  • The membrane potential changes, so calcium can enter the sperm, which makes the acrosomal reaction possible once the sperm binds ZP3.
  • Many proteins are phosphorylated, and hyperactivation begins: the tail's beat changes from wave-like to whip-like.

In short, capacitation removes the blocks to binding the oocyte and allows the acrosomal reaction. It is a transient event: it starts as the sperm travel through the uterus and happens mainly in the fallopian tube. That is why, soon after ejaculation, there is a stretch when sperm can't fertilize yet.

The fallopian tubes

At the distal end of each tube are the fimbriae, finger-like projections that capture the oocyte when the follicle ruptures at midcycle and bring it into the tube. Beating cilia and peristaltic contractions of the tube, a response to estrogen, his slide notes say, move it along. Fertilization most often happens in the distal fallopian tube.

Estrogen holds the embryo back, progesterone lets it in

Estrogen and progesterone act all through pregnancy, and between fertilization and implantation they pull in opposite directions. Just after midcycle, estrogen is still high, and estrogen promotes contraction and constriction. It constricts the opening of the uterus, where the fallopian tube meets it, which keeps the embryo from entering the uterus too soon. The delay gives the endometrium time to get ready.

When progesterone rises, the myometrium relaxes, and the blastocyst can move into the uterus and implant in the rich, well-vascularized lining of the luteal phase.

One rule runs through the whole lecture: estrogen contracts, progesterone relaxes. It comes back at labor, when the balance tips toward estrogen.

The first week: a timeline

Fertilization takes place within 24 hours of ovulation, typically on day 15 or 16 of the cycle. Rapid cell division follows. The blastocyst, about 100 cells, enters the uterine cavity about 4 days after ovulation, and implantation happens 5 to 7 days after ovulation. He stressed that these are ranges: "there's no definitive day." About 8 days after ovulation, the trophoblasts start secreting hCG, which he called the important part of his timeline slide.

The blastocyst

As the zygote divides, it passes through stages with their own names, and he said you don't need them: "I don't really care that you know all the different stages for my stuff... no, you don't have to know it." What matters is that implantation happens at the blastocyst stage. A blastocyst has many cells around a fluid-filled cavity, the blastocoele, and its outer layer is made of trophoblasts. The trophoblasts carry out implantation, and implantation is invasive: the blastocyst doesn't just stick to the wall, it has to "set up shop" and build a placenta to nourish the fetus.

Implantation

The blastocyst secretes three kinds of substances that help it implant: adhesion molecules, proteases and hormones, chiefly hCG. The uterus meets it halfway. Early pregnancy speeds up the decidualization of the endometrium, which makes it more receptive to the blastocyst. Decidualization is a set of changes: increased vascularity; increased glycogen, stored in vacuoles around the implanting blastocyst; and immune modulation, a local suppression of the immune system so it doesn't recognize the blastocyst as foreign and attack it. The luteal phase had already begun the vascular and glycogen changes; hormones from the blastocyst push them further.

His slide puts implantation in three steps.

  • Attachment, or adhesion. Adhesion molecules on the trophoblasts and on the endometrial cells bind the blastocyst firmly to the wall. He named L-selectin as one but said, "I don't care that you know them." The important thing is that attachment signals the trophoblasts to differentiate into two populations: cytotrophoblasts, the nurse cells that nourish the early embryo and give it structure, and syncytiotrophoblasts, the invaders.
  • Invasion. The syncytiotrophoblasts send out long protrusions that secrete proteases, which break down the matrix, so the blastocyst burrows deeper into the endometrial stroma.
  • Blastocyst differentiation. The blastocyst secretes paracrine factors that, along with progesterone, amplify the decidual reaction: the endometrial cells enlarge, accumulate glycogen and become decidual cells, which nourish the embryo until the placenta forms.

The syncytiotrophoblasts do three jobs: they are adhesive, invasive and endocrine, making hCG and human placental lactogen. They go on to help form the placenta.

hCG rescues the corpus luteum

Human chorionic gonadotropin, or hCG, is secreted by the trophoblasts about 8 days after ovulation. It "informs" the corpus luteum that fertilization has happened. "This is what rescues the corpus luteum." Without it, about 14 days after ovulation, the corpus luteum would regress into the corpus albicans, and estrogen and progesterone would fall abruptly. With it, the corpus luteum stays active, and under hCG's direction it increases its synthesis of progesterone and estrogen.

The effect reaches the pituitary too: LH and FSH release from the mother's anterior pituitary is suppressed. He tied this to the secondary amenorrhea of pregnancy, periods that had started and then stop: the cyclic waves of LH and FSH of a normal cycle are shut down. The goal is progesterone and estrogen kept high and steady, to nourish the developing placenta and fetus. His one-line summary: "hCG prevents the regression of corpus luteum, slows production of LH and FSH."

He credited hCG itself with slowing LH and FSH, and his slide says it "exerts negative feedback" on the maternal pituitary. Textbooks such as Costanzo credit the high estrogen and progesterone that hCG keeps flowing. Either way, LH and FSH stay low through pregnancy.

hCG is also what a pregnancy test measures: "it's very high, very quickly." His slide notes add that it can be found in urine or blood about 10 to 11 days after fertilization, and that it is highest toward the end of the first trimester, at about 10 weeks, then declines for the rest of pregnancy.

Two more points from the slide's notes. hCG can bind, weakly, to the TSH receptor, which can cause a transient gestational hyperthyroidism. Separately, estrogen raises thyroid-binding globulin, or TBG, so total T3 and T4 can double while free T3 and T4 don't rise much. The notes also mark pregnancy as an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic state, which comes back with human placental lactogen.

Corpus luteum first, then placenta

Rescued by hCG, the corpus luteum stays intact and makes most of the progesterone and estrogen during the first trimester, because the placenta isn't fully formed yet. The placenta begins developing shortly after implantation and is fully developed by the end of the first trimester. After that, it takes over the hormone production.

The placenta

The placenta has several jobs:

  • Nutrient and gas exchange: oxygen and nutrients in from the mother's blood, carbon dioxide and waste out.
  • Hormone production: hCG, progesterone, estrogen and human placental lactogen.
  • Immune protection: a selective barrier that protects the fetus from many infections while letting maternal antibodies through.
  • Waste removal: fetal waste goes into the mother's circulation, and she excretes it.
  • A regulatory barrier that controls what crosses from mother to fetus, drugs, nutrients and antibodies included.
  • Support for fetal development: growth, organ development and priming of the immune system.

He stressed the downside too: certain drugs and some viruses can pass from mother to fetus, so not everything that crosses is welcome. Most of his focus, though, is the placenta's hormones.

Human placental lactogen

Besides progesterone and estrogen, the placenta makes what he called accessory hormones, which prepare for life after birth or keep the pregnancy going. Human placental lactogen, or hPL, also called human chorionic somatomammotropin, affects the growth and development of breast tissue. It also has anti-insulin actions: it promotes lipolysis and the breakdown of carbohydrates and proteins, which keeps a continuous flow of nutrients going to the fetus.

That is part of why pregnancy is an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic state: the mother's tissues respond less to insulin, she uses more fat and spares glucose, and her insulin levels can run very high. Some mothers develop gestational diabetes. He called it multifactorial. Much of it is hormonal, since several placental and pregnancy hormones oppose insulin, but some women have a higher genetic predisposition, and no single hormone drives it. hPL is the one with research interest.

Relaxin

Relaxin is made by both the corpus luteum, in response to hCG, and the placenta. It inhibits myometrial contractions, keeping the uterus quiet, or quiescent, in early pregnancy, because "the last thing we want is a preterm delivery." It also relaxes the pelvic bones and ligaments and softens the cervix, and at the end of term it may help relax and thin the cervix for delivery.

Making progesterone and estrogen: mother, placenta and fetus

"Let's look at the main hormones that I care more about": the estrogens and progesterone. All of them start from cholesterol supplied by the mother, mostly from her diet.

Progesterone is simple: the placenta can make it on its own, and after the first trimester it supplies it to both mother and fetus.

Estrogen is trickier. The predominant estrogen of pregnancy is estriol. The three estrogens each belong to a stage of life: estradiol is the estrogen of the normal menstrual cycle, estrone the estrogen of menopause, and estriol the estrogen of pregnancy.

The placenta has cholesterol desmolase, so it can turn cholesterol into pregnenolone, and it has aromatase, the enzyme that turns androgens into estrogens. But it lacks 17,20 desmolase, and you need an androgen to make an estrogen. The fetus has that enzyme. So the work goes back and forth.

  • The placenta makes pregnenolone from the mother's cholesterol and passes it to the fetus.
  • The fetal adrenal gland, with its 17,20 desmolase, makes the androgen DHEA and adds a sulfate, giving DHEA sulfate. The sulfate keeps the androgen from virilizing the fetus.
  • The fetal liver hydroxylates it, giving 16-hydroxy DHEA sulfate.
  • Back in the placenta, aromatase converts it to estriol.

Because estriol needs a working fetal adrenal and liver, the mother's estriol level reflects the health of the fetus. The placenta can also use DHEA sulfate to make estradiol. The take-home, in his slide notes: to make estrogen, the placenta "needs help from the baby."

Parturition

Parturition is the delivery of the fetus, about 40 weeks after the onset of the last menstrual period; labor can of course come sooner. It takes several signals working together: estrogen, progesterone, oxytocin, prostaglandins and relaxin. Some are well understood; for others the evidence is still accumulating.

His slide lists the factors that start labor and keep it going.

  • Distention of the uterus as the fetus grows. He described it as a trigger: the baby gets so large that it pushes on the uterine wall, and the mechanical stretch sets off hormonal signals.
  • Upregulation of uterine receptors for PGF2 alpha and oxytocin. He said PGF2 alpha is really important in the uterus, tied to contraction and delivery.
  • Increased uterine sensitivity to estrogen and decreased sensitivity to progesterone. Estrogen increases uterine contractility and progesterone relaxes the myometrium, so as the ratio of estrogen to progesterone rises late in pregnancy, around 40 weeks, the myometrium shifts to a contracting state.
  • Increased uterine production of prostaglandins, PGE2 and PGF2 alpha. They raise intracellular calcium, and calcium drives muscle contraction, so contractions get stronger and more rhythmic. Prostaglandins also soften and thin the cervix; he singled out PGE2 for the softening.
  • Increased oxytocin secretion from the mother's posterior pituitary, "the big one." He asked the class where oxytocin comes from: the posterior pituitary, one of its two hormones. It is a powerful stimulant of uterine contraction, and it synergizes with the prostaglandins.

His slide notes describe the oxytocin loop as positive feedback: the contractions bring more oxytocin, not less, until they are strong enough to deliver the baby. And oxytocin keeps working after delivery. The contractions continue after the placenta is delivered, which prevents excessive bleeding: "oxytocin has a role both during active delivery and post-delivery." Relaxin, from earlier, helps change the cervix's tissue and thin it for delivery.

His slide notes also describe animal studies in which the fetus's adrenal axis surges cortisol and shifts the placenta toward estrogen. The human placenta lacks that enzyme, so the human trigger is different and not fully known. He didn't teach this part aloud.

Lactation: building the breast during pregnancy

The structures for lactation develop during pregnancy, driven by the high estrogen and progesterone made first by the corpus luteum and then by the placenta.

  • Estrogen: ductal and lobular growth and ductal branching, and more fat deposition in the breast. Breast fat expresses aromatase, so it makes estrogen locally.
  • Progesterone: increases the number of alveoli, the milk-producing structures.
  • Prolactin: rises, especially later in pregnancy, and increases the enzymes that produce milk.
  • Cortisol: also increases the milk enzymes.

"What you should know is that a lot of prolactin's effects during pregnancy are inhibited. They're kind of antagonized by progesterone." Progesterone antagonizes prolactin, especially locally in the breast, so the high placental progesterone suppresses milk production. There may be a little milk, but full milk production doesn't start until after delivery. The development continues all the same, setting the stage.

After delivery: prolactin makes milk, oxytocin lets it down

Once the baby and placenta are delivered, progesterone falls, and prolactin's brake comes off. Prolactin then drives full milk production in the alveoli. Around each alveolus are myoepithelial cells, which respond to oxytocin by contracting, and that squeezes the milk out: milk letdown. "Prolactin sets the stage and creates all the milk products. Oxytocin is going to stimulate milk letdown."

His shorthand: prolactin, milk production; oxytocin, milk letdown. A question that swaps the two is the obvious trap.

How prolactin and oxytocin are controlled

Normally, prolactin is tonically inhibited: without a baby to feed, there's no need for milk. The hypothalamus does it by constantly releasing dopamine, "a potent inhibitor of prolactin release from the anterior pituitary." So in most people, prolactin stays low.

After delivery the brake is released. Suckling decreases dopamine, and he added that the sounds and sight of the baby and the emotions around delivery can lower it too. With dopamine down, the anterior pituitary releases prolactin, and prolactin releasing factor pushes it up further. Low dopamine means high prolactin. Some prolactin is made during pregnancy, but this whole circuit turns on after the baby is delivered.

Suckling also makes the hypothalamus produce oxytocin, which is carried to the posterior pituitary and released into the blood to reach the breast.

"One thing that I want to highlight": prolactin inhibits GnRH, gonadotropin-releasing hormone. Less GnRH means less LH and FSH and lower sex steroids downstream, which is why high prolactin brings amenorrhea. It is the same mechanism as hyperprolactinemia, high prolactin from any cause, and it is why a breastfeeding mother's periods often stop. On this slide, he said, "mainly focus on this side of things. Dopamine being important."

Dr. Pius Fasinu (Pharmacology and Toxicology) gave Lecture 18 on Wednesday, November 11, at 1 pm. His deck, "Pharmacology of Estrogens and Androgens," reviews where the sex steroids come from and what they do, then covers the drugs: the androgens and anti-androgens, the estrogens, the selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs), the aromatase inhibitors, the progestins and the anti-progestins. He worked through five short cases with the class, two of them set in the dental chair. He said he would spend his time on the drugs, since the physiology was covered in your physiology lectures. These notes follow the recording and slides.

His objectives: recall the physiologic effects of estrogens and androgens; list examples of estrogenic drugs, SERMs, androgenic drugs and anti-androgenic drugs; discuss the mechanism of each drug class; and highlight their therapeutic uses and safety concerns. His advice: "If you're able to do those, the names will suggest to you how they work, based on their classes." The drugs his slides highlight in red are goserelin, finasteride, dutasteride, flutamide, bicalutamide, tamoxifen, raloxifene, anastrozole, progesterone, hydroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel and ulipristal. His summary slide adds testosterone, DHEA, estradiol, estrone and ethinyl estradiol.

His opening case: testosterone or estrogen?

He opened with a quick case: for each condition, which hormone should be avoided, testosterone or estrogen?

  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH): avoid testosterone, which fuels prostate enlargement.
  • Breast cancer: avoid estrogen in women, and also testosterone in men. Breast cancer is rare in men, but it happens.
  • A history of thromboembolism (a deep vein clot or a pulmonary embolism): avoid estrogen. "I think it's the most serious and most common side effect of estrogens," he said: estrogens disturb clot formation, so abnormal clotting is typical of estrogen therapy.
  • Pregnancy: testosterone has the most adverse effect. He called it an absolute contraindication in pregnancy.

He added that there may be a few instances where estrogen is used in a pregnant woman, but his estrogen slide lists pregnancy as a contraindication to estrogens too. In his case, testosterone is the answer for pregnancy.

Where the sex hormones come from

His overview chart traces each hormone back to the pituitary: the hypothalamus sends releasing hormones to the anterior pituitary, whose FSH and LH drive the ovaries and testes to make progesterone, estradiol and testosterone. This lecture's hormones are progesterone, testosterone and estrogen, "which is formed from testosterone."

The biosynthetic pathway is complex, and his slide is an extract of it. Cholesterol is turned, in several steps, into DHEA, dehydroepiandrosterone, an important precursor. DHEA is converted to androstenedione (or androstenediol) and then to testosterone. DHEAS is the sulfate form of DHEA.

His slide's abbreviation table lists DHEA as "dihydrotestosterone." He corrected it in class: DHEA is dehydroepiandrosterone, the precursor; DHT is dihydrotestosterone, the active androgen; DHEAS is the sulfate of DHEA.

DHEA matters because it is sold over the counter as a supplement (as prasterone). Many older men take it during andropause, which is like menopause in men, to supplement their testosterone, since it is the precursor of testosterone. It is controversial: every testosterone product is a Schedule III controlled drug except DHEA, which he said has escaped that regulation.

Once testosterone is made, it has two fates, and a drug class is built on each.

  • 5-alpha-reductase reduces testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, or DHT. The name tells you what it does: it is a reductase. "Dihydrotestosterone is the active testosterone." Reducing testosterone is its bioactivation, so to lower androgen activity you can give a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, and no DHT is made.
  • Aromatase aromatizes one of testosterone's rings, turning it into estradiol (and androstenedione into estrone). From estradiol the body can form estrone and estriol. Aromatase inhibitors are popular in treating certain cancers where you don't want estrogenic activity.

When there is enough DHT in the body, it feeds back negatively on the hypothalamus and the pituitary.

How testosterone is controlled

His regulation slide: the hypothalamus releases GnRH (also called LHRH) in a pulsatile way, a short burst and then a long pause. GnRH makes the pituitary release FSH and LH, which drive the testes: they make testosterone and support spermatogenesis. In the target tissues, steroid 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, which drives male maturation and development and the growth of bone and muscle. Remember the pulses: they explain the GnRH drugs later.

What testosterone does

He went through the physiological effects quickly, as physiology you have seen:

  • Differentiation of the male fetus from the female, and development of the male reproductive organs before birth and of the secondary sex traits at puberty.
  • Maintenance of reproductive function, mainly sperm formation.
  • It decreases the plasma binding globulins: CBG (corticosteroid-binding globulin), TBG (thyroxine-binding globulin), SHBG (sex hormone-binding globulin) and transferrin. These proteins, made in the liver, carry hormones in the plasma until they reach their target, and a hormone exists in equilibrium between bound and free. Androgens and their analogs lower the plasma levels of these carriers.
  • It increases skin thickness, secretions, pigmentation and circulation.
  • Retention of water and electrolytes, which is why testosterone is not a good drug for people with ongoing cardiovascular problems, including hypertension.
  • It decreases circulating HDL, the good cholesterol, so it is also not good for people with cholesterol problems.
  • It increases protein synthesis and muscle mass, anabolic especially in the upper body. That is why androgens are abused to build muscle in sports, which is not legal and counts as cheating.
  • Erythropoiesis: it increases red blood cell formation, so androgens can treat refractory anemia.
  • Growth: DHT stimulates growth, and estradiol limits it by closing the epiphyses.
  • Increased libido.

The growth point is why aromatase deficiency matters. Estradiol is made from testosterone by aromatase, so a man born without aromatase cannot make estradiol, and his epiphyses don't close on time. "They're the ones that grow very tall": long bones, but weak, osteoporotic bones with a high risk of osteoporosis. His slide's treatment is estradiol.

How the sex steroids act

All the hormones in this block are very lipophilic, and they all bind nuclear receptors: thyroxine, the corticosteroids and the sex steroids alike. In the plasma they travel bound: the sex hormones to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), while a corticosteroid binds CBG. Only the free hormone reaches the receptor. Testosterone or DHT enters the cell and binds the androgen receptor (DHT is the main ligand, and testosterone binds it too), and the hormone-receptor complex changes gene expression. Because the effect goes through gene transcription, it takes time. Estradiol acts the same way through estrogen receptors.

The androgen drugs

Testosterone itself is the natural hormone, the standard the others are compared with. It is Schedule III and comes in many forms: IV or depot injection, an implant (Testopel), a buccal tablet (Striant), a nasal gel (Natesto), topical gels (AndroGel, Testim, Vogelxo) and a transdermal patch (Androderm).

Testosterone cypionate (Depo-Testosterone) is the one he said is dispensed and injected: an intramuscular depot, released very slowly, injected about once a week or once a month. Testosterone enanthate (Delatestryl) and testosterone undecanoate (Aveed) are other injectable forms.

The table's second column compares each drug's androgenic and anabolic activity, because most indications want one or the other. Is the patient deficient in androgenic activity, or do you want anabolic activity, for example for unexplained weight loss with some cancers? Testosterone and its injectable forms are all 1 to 1: the form doesn't change the anabolic activity. For a strongly anabolic drug you would look at the other analogs (fluoxymesterone, oxymetholone, nandrolone, oxandrolone), which are more anabolic than androgenic; oxymetholone and nandrolone also raise red blood cell counts in anemia. Uses and adverse effects of androgens

Their mechanism is activation of nuclear androgen receptors. The uses on his slide:

  • Replacement in male hypogonadism, for men who don't produce enough.
  • Some breast tumors in women.
  • Anabolic effects, when clinically indicated.
  • Refractory anemias, through erythropoiesis.
  • Osteoporosis ("not the best drug," he said, but it can be used in women).
  • Growth.
  • Reversing the effects of male aging, andropause.

The side effects are more pronounced in women and children, so avoid testosterone in women as much as possible.

  • Women: hirsutism, including facial hair, a deepened voice, an enlarged clitoris and smaller breasts: the changes you expect in boys at puberty. These can be irreversible with prolonged use.
  • Men: sleep apnea ("a big problem"), priapism, increased sex drive, and feminization: gynecomastia and azoospermia. He said the feminization is believed to come from testosterone being converted to estradiol.
  • Both: acne, edema, hepatotoxicity, jaundice, lower HDL and higher LDL, dependence, aggressiveness and psychosis.

"I think the most important side effect of testosterone everyone needs to also know is hepatotoxicity." People are screened for it, and a patient who already has a liver problem doesn't get testosterone.

A counseling point he gives when dispensing testosterone, especially the cream: apply it last thing at night, before bed. It is lipophilic and passes through the skin very easily (the route is transdermal, not just topical), so if you hug your child after putting it on, the child can get testosterone into their system. The same goes for women.

Contraindications and cautions: pregnancy or planning to become pregnant, heart or liver disease, men with prostate or breast cancer, and extreme caution in children (and women). In class he summed it up as pregnancy and liver disease.

The anti-androgens: three ways to lower androgen activity

"This can be confusing, so often I take time to explain it." An anti-androgen either blocks testosterone at its receptor, prevents its activation to DHT, or shuts down its production. That gives three classes.

GnRH analogs

The GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) analogs are goserelin (Zoladex), the one he highlighted and one of the most common on the market, leuprolide (Eligard, Lupron), nafarelin (Synarel), triptorelin (Trelstar) and histrelin (Supprelin).

The paradox: GnRH should be pro-androgen, because it drives LH and testosterone. The body releases it in pulses, a short burst and then a long pause with no release. These drugs are slow-release, long-acting analogs, so they stimulate the pituitary cells continuously, and eventually the cells switch off: FSH and LH secretion is suppressed, and with it testosterone. "That's the only way it's going to make sense to you": given this way, a GnRH analog works as an anti-androgen.

Uses: primarily prostate cancer (what Zoladex is used for), and also benign prostatic hyperplasia, precocious puberty (signs of early puberty), chemical castration and prepubertal cryptorchidism (testes that have not descended). Side effects are mostly anti-sex-hormonal: impotence and gynecomastia, what you expect in hypogonadism.

5-alpha-reductase inhibitors

Testosterone is not very active until it is reduced to dihydrotestosterone, so that reduction is its bioactivation. If you don't want androgenic activity, inhibit the enzyme that does it, 5-alpha-reductase. The two he highlighted: finasteride (Proscar, Propecia) and dutasteride (Avodart).

Uses: benign prostatic hyperplasia and alopecia. Proscar is important for two reasons: it treats BPH, and a side effect was that it makes people grow hair. So a lower strength was approved for hair loss as Propecia. Proscar and Propecia are the same drug, finasteride: "The difference between Proscar and Propecia is the dose, the strength of the tablet," and the indication. The high strength is for BPH and the low strength for alopecia. (He wasn't sure of the numbers in class; Proscar is 5 mg and Propecia 1 mg.)

Side effects: gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction.

Androgen receptor antagonists

The third class is the one you would naturally think of: drugs that compete with testosterone at its receptor. He highlighted flutamide (Eulexin) and bicalutamide (Casodex); nilutamide (Nilandron) and enzalutamide (Xtandi) are the others on the slide. Mechanism: competitive antagonism of androgen receptors. Uses: prostate cancer in men, and excess androgens in women. Side effects: GI disturbances (least with bicalutamide), gynecomastia and hepatotoxicity.

His advice for all three classes: "Try to familiarize with those highlighted examples. That should be enough for you."

For testosterone to estradiol, it would be aromatase: "When you aromatize the ring, it becomes estrogen."

The natural estrogens

There are three natural estrogens:

  • Estradiol (E2), made in the ovary: the main estrogen.
  • Estrone (E1), made in the liver and peripheral tissues.
  • Estriol (E3), also made in the liver and peripheral tissues.

When aromatase converts testosterone you get estradiol (and from androstenedione, estrone), and these two can be converted to estriol.

Estrone and estriol are conjugated and secreted into the bile, then reactivated and reabsorbed in the gut: enterohepatic recirculation. Oral estrogens have more effects on the liver, including an increase in clotting factors.

The mechanism is like the androgens'. In plasma, estrogen is in equilibrium between free and bound to SHBG and albumin. Free estrogen binds the estrogen receptor, found in the cytoplasm and the nucleus. A receptor bound in the cytoplasm moves into the nucleus, where the complex alters gene expression.

What estrogen does

  • Female maturation: development of the vagina, uterus and secondary sex traits.
  • Endometrium: growth of the uterine muscle and development of the uterine lining.
  • Metabolic: estrogen increases HDL, unlike testosterone, which lowers it, and it increases triglycerides, with a slight increase in LDL on his slide. Because of the triglycerides, he said, estrogens are not good for people with cardiovascular issues.
  • It maintains the skin and blood vessels in women. That is why doctors sometimes prescribe oral contraceptives to teenagers, even in high school: not for contraception, but for very bad skin as they approach puberty.
  • It antagonizes PTH-mediated bone calcium resorption, which protects bone.
  • Coagulation: it increases production of clotting factors 2, 7, 9 and 10 and decreases antithrombin III.

That last point is the one he kept coming back to: "Drugs that are estrogenic, even those that are anti-estrogenic, they tend to increase clotting factors, and that's why they have a problem with thrombosis": pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis and other clots.

His second slide of effects adds an increase in progesterone receptor synthesis and in libido, then a list he skipped ("several other effects, very similar to testosterone. I don't want to bother you with that"): more ACTH, well-being, edema, closing the epiphyses, a rise in plasma CBG, TBG, SHBG and transferrin (the opposite of testosterone), potentiation of progesterone, and inhibition of FSH and LH at high concentrations.

Therapeutic estrogens

The indications: primary hypogonadism in women (as testosterone is used in men), postmenopausal hormone therapy, oral contraceptives, suppressing ovulation in intractable dysmenorrhea or hirsutism, and fertility treatments.

He made the pairing explicit. For hormone therapy in menopause, "that's what Premarin is for. That's estrone, and not estradiol. Ethinyl estradiol, that is for contraception."

His figure of estrogen as hormone therapy in menopause sets the good effects against the bad. Good: it strengthens bones, improves cholesterol (lower LDL, higher HDL) and reduces menopausal symptoms such as hot flashes. Bad: it increases the risk of breast cancer, of uterine cancer and of blood clots. The figure's footnote: the added uterine cancer risk can be reduced or eliminated by giving progesterone along with estrogen.

The figure says estrogen lowers LDL, while the effects slide says a slight increase in LDL. The point the lecture leans on is HDL: estrogen raises it, testosterone lowers it.

Estrogen's adverse effects, contraindications and interactions

Common side effects: nausea, fluid retention, breakthrough bleeding, a change in menstrual flow and breast tenderness. Fluid retention is common to both androgens and estrogens, and it worsens hypertension, heart failure and other cardiovascular problems.

Serious effects: thromboembolic complications, endometrial carcinoma, breast carcinoma and hypertension. In men, estrogen causes feminization of the genitalia and impotence. "I can't say it enough": clots are very well known with estrogens.

Contraindications: pregnancy, incomplete bone growth, undiagnosed genital bleeding, stroke, thrombophlebitis or thromboembolic disease, heart disease, and women with a family history of breast or uterine cancer (the BRCA gene). A history counts however old it is: a heart attack or any clotting event, stroke included, "it doesn't matter, 10 years ago": if you see it in a case, the patient should not take any estrogen product. And a family history counts too: it doesn't have to be the patient herself.

Drug interactions: estrogens decrease the efficacy of oral anticoagulants, because they increase the production of clotting factors, and of hypoglycemic agents.

His slide writes "thrombolytic complications," and he said it aloud too, but the meaning is clots forming (thrombotic or thromboembolic events), not clots dissolving.

SERMs: why a drug can be selective

For androgens there were three ways to block them. For estrogen, the main class is the selective estrogen receptor modulators, or SERMs. Estrogen has two receptor subtypes, ER-alpha and ER-beta, and different tissues express them at different levels: differential tissue expression. Binding to DNA and transcription factors also depends on the shape the receptor takes. So one drug can be pro-estrogenic in one tissue, partly estrogenic in another and anti-estrogenic in a third. That is why they are called modulators: an antagonist in one tissue and an agonist in another.

Tamoxifen

Tamoxifen (Nolvadex) is one of the most popular SERMs, used to treat breast cancer. In the breast it binds the estrogen receptor as an antagonist, so the breast cells stop proliferating, which lowers cancer risk. In the uterus the receptor subtype is different, and tamoxifen activates it: endometrial cells proliferate, and the risk of uterine cancer rises. His figure of tamoxifen's effects: good, it reduces breast cancer risk, lowers LDL and strengthens bones; bad, it increases uterine cancer risk and blood clot risk.

Not every breast cancer is fueled by estrogen, so the tumor is tested first. When the cancer cells overexpress estrogen receptors (they are ER-positive), the growth is being fueled by estrogen, and an anti-estrogen will work: "That is the only time you give tamoxifen." His slide: tamoxifen is most effective in ER-positive tumors, with about a 50 percent response. It is not for indiscriminate use in every breast cancer.

Raloxifene

Raloxifene (Evista), close to tamoxifen, is used mainly to treat osteoporosis in postmenopausal women: it has a preference for the receptors in bone. It has a high affinity for both ER-alpha and ER-beta, and it does not cause proliferation of the endometrium or of breast tumor cells. Its side effect: a 2- to 3-fold increase in the risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Agonist or antagonist, these modulators should be avoided in patients with a history of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.

Clomiphene

Clomiphene (Clomid) is used to induce ovulation: "kind of first-line drug for fertility." It is a weak agonist and strong antagonist at the estrogen receptors. By blocking them, it opposes the negative feedback of the body's own estrogen, so the LH and FSH pulses grow larger, and the ovary is driven to ovulate. It works in women whose hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is intact.

Adverse effects: multiple births, because several eggs can be released (twins, triplets, even quadruplets), and ovarian cysts.

How he read it: some, like tamoxifen, stimulate the uterus, and others don't; tamoxifen and raloxifene both act like estrogen on bone; none of them stimulates breast cells; and none of them inhibits ovulation. The same receptors are expressed at different levels in different cells, which is why the drugs have different uses: "So again, tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for osteoporosis, Clomid, that is for, to stimulate ovulation."

The full table also lists toremifene (Fareston) and ospemifene (Osphena), which match tamoxifen; bazedoxifene (Duavee), which matches raloxifene; and fulvestrant (Faslodex), which matches clomiphene. "They are rarely used," he said.

Aromatase inhibitors

Instead of blocking the estrogen receptor, you can stop estradiol from being made. Testosterone is aromatized to estradiol by aromatase, a natural enzyme, so an aromatase inhibitor inhibits the conversion of testosterone to estradiol. The most popular is anastrozole (Arimidex); letrozole (Femara) and exemestane (Aromasin) are the others. Use: breast cancer treatment.

Adverse effects: hot flashes, GI disturbances, CNS disturbances (anxiety, confusion, depression) and thromboembolism. He said these drugs share estrogen-type side effects whether they act for or against estrogen: "At least you should be able to remember hot flashes... and thromboembolism." Contraindications: hepatic damage and premenopausal women.

The hot flashes come from the fall in estrogen, the same reason they come at menopause. The slide doesn't say why premenopausal women are excluded; the textbook reason is that before menopause the ovaries make most of the estrogen, and lowering it raises FSH and LH, which drive the ovaries harder.

Progesterone

Progesterone is made in the adrenal cortex, the corpus luteum, the placenta and the testes. He assumed you know its physiology; the action he stressed is the maturation of the endometrium. His slide lists others he didn't go through: it stimulates lipase, glycogen storage and insulin activity; competitively inhibits mineralocorticoid receptors, so less sodium is reabsorbed; raises body temperature; increases the breathing response to carbon dioxide; drives the alveolobular development of the breast; and increases urinary nitrogen excretion.

The progestin drugs

The progestins are analogs of progesterone. He highlighted progesterone itself (Prometrium), hydroxyprogesterone and levonorgestrel. The slide also lists medroxyprogesterone (Provera), desogestrel, norgestimate, norethindrone, drospirenone, megestrol (Megace) and dienogest, and two combinations: etonogestrel with ethinyl estradiol (NuvaRing), and medroxyprogesterone with conjugated estrogens (Prempro).

Progestins are what we use for contraception, regular and emergency. Many women cannot take estrogen: a family history of thromboembolism, or a history of breast or uterine cancer. If they choose contraception, they have to avoid the pills that contain ethinyl estradiol and take a progestin-only contraceptive. Levonorgestrel is the most common progestin in oral contraceptives, and Plan B, the emergency contraceptive, is just a high strength of levonorgestrel.

His Cases 3, 4 and 5

Case 3: in a health-education talk, a teenager asks about combination versus progestin-only contraceptives. Of ethinyl estradiol, estradiol, levonorgestrel and estrone, which has the least estrogenic effect? Levonorgestrel, a progestin; the other three are estrogens.

Case 4: a 38-year-old man taking finasteride for androgenic alopecia comes in for a crown and mentions decreased libido and mild breast tenderness. Which enzyme does finasteride inhibit? 5-alpha-reductase, one of the two examples he highlighted: it prevents the conversion of testosterone to its active form. Gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction are the class's side effects.

Case 5: a 62-year-old woman with osteoporosis takes raloxifene and comes in because a tooth extraction site is healing slowly. Which added risk, like estrogen therapy's, should the dentist be aware of? Thromboembolic events during immobilization. "Regardless of if they are antagonists or agonists," these drugs share estrogen's side effects. Gingival hyperplasia, immunosuppression and low calcium were the case's wrong choices.

The pharmacology of progestins

Mechanism: activation of the progestin receptor, which suppresses FSH (and LH and estradiol) secretion, preventing ovulation.

Uses: replacement, contraception before and after intercourse (pre- and post-coital), dysmenorrhea, endometriosis, precocious puberty and premenstrual syndrome.

Adverse effects: hypertension, lower HDL (an androgenic effect) and cancer risk, especially combined with estrogen. Contraindications: pregnancy desired in the near future, and hypertension.

Two slides seem to pull in opposite directions: the hormone therapy figure says adding progesterone lowers estrogen's uterine cancer risk, and the progestin slide lists cancer risk, especially combined with estrogen. Both hold: the progestin protects the endometrium, while combined hormone therapy carries other cancer risk (in standard texts, mainly breast cancer).

Anti-progestins and emergency contraception

Ulipristal (Ella), the one he highlighted, is a progestin receptor antagonist. Mifepristone (Mifeprex, Korlym) is an antagonist at both the progestin and the glucocorticoid receptors. The slide's use for them: post-coital (emergency) contraception. Contraindications: pregnancy desired in the near future, and Addison disease. Mifepristone blocks cortisol's receptor, and a patient with Addison disease already makes too little cortisol.

Emergency contraception, side by side. Plan B is a high dose of levonorgestrel, a progestin; ulipristal is an antagonist: "The difference is this. This is an antagonist." Both have the same indication. The differences he called "probably more important": Plan B has to be used within 72 hours, while ulipristal can be used up to 120 hours, 5 days; and ulipristal is prescription only, while Plan B is sold without a prescription.

Summary: the drugs to know

His summary slide names the drugs to know in each class: testosterone and DHEA (androgens); finasteride and flutamide (anti-androgens); estradiol, estrone and ethinyl estradiol (estrogens); tamoxifen and raloxifene (SERMs); progesterone and levonorgestrel (progestins); and ulipristal, the emergency contraceptive (anti-progestins). Add the other red drugs: goserelin, dutasteride, bicalutamide, anastrozole and hydroxyprogesterone, with testosterone cypionate and clomiphene, which he stressed aloud.

"Pay attention to those drugs that I highlight in the slides, and you should be fine."

In the dental chair

His two dental cases: a man on finasteride may mention a lower libido or breast tenderness, the side effects of blocking 5-alpha-reductase; and a woman on raloxifene, like a patient on estrogen, carries a higher risk of a clot, especially while she is immobilized after a procedure.
