Plasma cell neoplasms

Plasma cells are the antibody-making end of the B-cell line, so their tumors, which he called B-cell neoplasms, make monoclonal immunoglobulin. He said they can be solitary, in one place, usually a rib or the spine, or multifocal, in the bone marrow, and may come with end-organ damage. Under the microscope the plasma cells have eccentric nuclei.

  • A plasmacytoma is a solitary tumor of clonal plasma cells. Patients present with pain, swelling or a fracture at that spot, or with spinal cord compression. The standard treatment of an extramedullary plasmacytoma is radiation to the involved field.
  • Plasma cell myeloma is a bone marrow-based, multifocal proliferation of plasma cells. Multiple myeloma is plasma cell myeloma, usually with a monoclonal immunoglobulin in the serum or urine, plus either organ damage from the disease or, without it, lab or imaging findings that predict organ damage within 2 years. It is considered incurable for most patients.

He went through the findings: lytic bone lesions (punched-out holes in the bone on radiographs); an M-spike on protein electrophoresis, the monoclonal protein as one tall, narrow band; the CRAB features of organ damage, which stand for hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia and bone lesions; and rouleaux on the blood smear, red cells stacked like coins, because the large amount of immunoglobulin protein makes them stick together ("it makes this sticky"). Aloud he listed the clinical findings as hypercalcemia, renal impairment and anemia, with the lytic bone; the CRAB chart on his slide is a picture.

In the jaw, myeloma's lytic lesions are radiolucencies and its calcium is high, so it can look like the brown tumors of hyperparathyroidism from Lecture A. The monoclonal protein, the rouleaux and the anemia point to myeloma.

Peripheral T-cell lymphoma

He skipped this slide ("I'm going to skip peripheral T-cell lymphoma"), giving only its gist: very aggressive T-cell lymphomas, whose markers say they are T cells, in patients who typically have B symptoms and don't necessarily respond to chemotherapy; the cells are large. The slide's detail follows. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL, NOS) is a mixed category: the mature T-cell lymphomas, in nodes or outside them, that don't fit a specific type. It is diagnosed nearly always in adults, and most present with advanced disease, usually lymphadenopathy and B symptoms, often with the marrow, liver, spleen, skin or GI tract involved. It carries T-cell markers, more often CD4 than CD8. These are aggressive lymphomas, with a poor response to therapy, frequent relapses and low survival.

Mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome

He went through these quickly: "I'm not going to go over in much detail, but know that these are the most common types of cutaneous lymphomas that are involving the skin, and that they have an indolent course." Mycosis fungoides is a T-cell lymphoma of the skin; with Sézary syndrome it is the most common type of cutaneous lymphoma, more than half of cases. Its lesions evolve in sequence: patches, then plaques, then tumors. They can be one or many; when localized they favor sun-protected skin, the flexures (armpits and groin) and the lower trunk and buttocks, a "bathing-trunk" distribution. Under the microscope, small to medium-sized T cells with a clear halo and hyperchromatic, hyperconvoluted ("cerebriform") nuclei line up along the basal layer and infiltrate the epidermis: they are epidermotropic. The course is indolent, over years or decades, with lesions that persist and grow slowly. It can appear at any age, peaking in the late fifties.

Sézary syndrome is defined by a triad: erythroderma (red skin over most of the body), generalized lymphadenopathy, and clonal T cells with cerebriform nuclei, Sézary cells, in the skin, the lymph nodes and the peripheral blood. He called it the aggressive version, with the blood and the nodes involved; the cerebriform nuclei in the blood help confirm it, and the node involvement can be subtle. Unlike mycosis fungoides, it is aggressive: the 5-year survival is 10 to 30 percent, and most patients die of opportunistic infections.

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma is a lymphoma of NK-cell or T-cell lineage that damages and destroys blood vessels, with prominent necrosis, and a very strong association with EBV. It begins in the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx, Waldeyer ring or epiglottis. From the nose it can grow out into the face or erode the nasal floor, destroying and perforating the hard palate, the picture once called "lethal midline granuloma". A dentist may be the first to see it. He covered it briefly, as time ran short ("you guys may come across this"): EBV-associated lymphomas of the midline of the palate, perforating lesions from a very aggressive lymphoma causing necrosis.

It occurs mainly in eastern Asia and among the Indigenous peoples of Central and South America, and is uncommon in Europe and the United States. The tumor grows diffusely around and into vessel walls (angiocentric and angiodestructive), commonly with coagulative necrosis. With chemotherapy and radiotherapy, the 5-year survival in early-stage disease is over 70 percent.

Chronic myeloid leukemia

"The main chronic leukemia that you need to know is chronic myeloid leukemia." Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (the slides join the two names with a double colon), with too many neutrophils, a neutrophilic granulocytosis. At diagnosis, 90 to 95 percent carry the reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, t(9;22), which makes the shortened chromosome 22 called the Philadelphia chromosome.

The fusion gene makes a tyrosine kinase that is always on. Its increased activity is necessary and sufficient to cause the chronic phase, by keeping several signaling pathways switched on.

Its phases. In the chronic phase, the neoplastic cells stay mostly in the blood, marrow, spleen and liver. More than 95 percent are diagnosed in the chronic phase, which comes on insidiously; some patients have no symptoms and are found on a routine blood count. Untreated, most progress within a few years to an advanced phase: declining health, fever and weight loss, and worse anemia, low platelets, a rising white count and a growing spleen. In the blast phase, blasts can infiltrate any site outside the marrow, especially the spleen, liver, lymph nodes, skin and soft tissues.

Its blood and marrow. The white count is high, from 12,000 to 1,000,000 per microliter, with a median of about 80,000 (the slide writes it as 12 to 1,000 times 10 to the 9th per liter). The cells are mostly neutrophils at every stage of maturation, with peaks at the myelocytes and the segmented neutrophils, not blasts. He put it as the full pattern of maturation, from early blasts all the way to neutrophils, all increased in the blood and the marrow, with a count high enough to separate it from a reactive one, such as an infection. The marrow is hypercellular, more than 95 percent cellular, with granulocytes at every stage, and his slide shows small, hypolobated megakaryocytes. The karyotype shows the Philadelphia chromosome.

Its treatment. Knowing the abnormal signal led to drugs that block it, the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, of which imatinib (Gleevec) was the first and is first-line therapy. It targets the enzymatically active part of the p210 BCR-ABL1 protein: it competes with ATP for the active site and so prevents the kinase from activating. He put it as blocking the binding site, so BCR-ABL1 can't bind its substrate and drive the cell to proliferate. In this era of kinase inhibitors, the most important sign of prognosis is the response to treatment, measured in the blood count, the chromosomes and the molecular test.

Blasts and Auer rods

"Blasts are the hallmark of acute leukemia." But they are not found only there. In lower numbers, under 20 percent, they appear in other myeloid disorders that can come before AML, such as a myelodysplastic syndrome. And outside the newborn period, blasts in the peripheral blood are always abnormal.

An Auer rod is a red-blue, needle-like inclusion in the cytoplasm of some myeloblasts, formed from abnormal granules that fuse. Aloud he called them cytoplasmic inclusions of a myeloid blast. An Auer rod marks the blast as myeloid, which is why Auer rods exclude ALL.

His slide adds that Auer rods are lysosomal and acid phosphatase-positive; textbooks (Robbins, the WHO) stress that they are myeloperoxidase-positive. He didn't mention either stain aloud, and no question asks.

Acute promyelocytic leukemia

He named two acute leukemias "you need to know", and this is the first. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a type of AML in which abnormal promyelocytes predominate. Its genetic hallmark is a balanced translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17, t(15;17), which fuses the promyelocytic leukemia gene, PML, with the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene, RARA. The fusion protein, PML-RARA (written with a double colon on the slides), causes the disease by impairing myeloid differentiation: maturation stops at the promyelocyte.

The cells look the part: abnormal promyelocytes whose cytoplasm is packed with large, dense granules staining bright pink, red or purple, and distinctive cells holding bundles of Auer rods scattered through the cytoplasm. He showed numerous Auer rods in them.

He gave two reasons to know it. The danger: "they have certain clinical presentations that can kill the patient." APL is frequently associated with a coagulopathy and a risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), which can cause early death: "you clot everywhere at the same time, which makes you at risk of clotting and bleeding." In the mouth, that means bleeding gums, petechiae and bruising.

The good news, "the treatment for it is excellent compared to other acute leukemias": all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide (ATRA plus ATO), without conventional chemotherapy, is highly effective and largely curative for low- and intermediate-risk APL. The retinoic acid lets the blocked promyelocytes mature.

Acute monocytic leukemia and the gums

The second acute leukemia he said you need: "the thing that I want you to know is that they can have extramedullary disease presentation in the oral cavity." Acute monocytic leukemia is an AML with monocytic differentiation and no defining genetic abnormality. The marrow is extensively infiltrated by immature, intermediate-sized to large cells with irregularly lobulated to kidney-shaped (reniform) nuclei, fine chromatin and distinct nucleoli. Flow cytometry shows two or more monocytic markers.

Patients present with symptoms of their cytopenias, with disease outside the marrow, or both, and the oral cavity is one of those places. AML that forms a mass outside the marrow is called a myeloid sarcoma (extramedullary AML). In the mouth it shows as gingival hypertrophy: swollen gums infiltrated by leukemic cells. His slides cite two case reports, one of them a myeloid sarcoma of the mandibular gingiva that was the relapse of a treated AML. This is what his objective means by the extramedullary presentation of acute leukemia. He said a biopsy of those gums can look a little like lymphoma, but studies confirm the leukemia, and the marrow is diffusely full of blasts.

Swollen gums in a patient who is tired, pale and bruising call for a blood count.

B-lymphoblastic leukemia

For B-ALL and T-ALL he said: "You don't need to know a ton of detail other than some of the demographic information for this." They occur mostly in children, the most common acute leukemia of childhood, though they can occur in adults. The diagnosis doesn't strictly need 20 percent blasts if other features, such as the cytogenetics, make it, and most children do well, after the testing sorts them by risk. The rest of this section is from his slides. B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL/LBL, also called precursor B-cell ALL) is a neoplasm of precursor lymphoid cells committed to the B-cell line. When it involves the marrow, and usually the blood, it is B-ALL; when nodes or other tissues are the primary sites, it is B-lymphoblastic lymphoma.

It is diagnosed by morphology and flow cytometry (the blasts essentially always carry B-lineage antigens) and classified further by its cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities, which carry prognostic and treatment implications. No set blast number is required, although a diagnosis with under 20 percent blasts is made with caution.

B-ALL occurs mainly in children: 75 percent of patients are under 6, and it is the most common leukemia of childhood. The incidence is bimodal, with a second, smaller peak in the fifth decade of life (the 40s). It usually presents with bone marrow failure: low platelets, anemia, low neutrophils, or all three. The lymphoblasts range from small cells with scant cytoplasm to larger ones with more pale blue-gray cytoplasm, sometimes vacuolated. With risk-stratified treatment, more than 90 percent of children reach long-term remission; adults do less well, because of harsher biology and the toxicity of treatment.

T-lymphoblastic leukemia and lymphoma

T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma is the same idea in the T-cell line: he said the testing confirms the cells are T cells, and the outcomes are a little worse than B-ALL's, but still generally good. The lymphoblasts have a very high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and the involved marrow looks very blue. It is called T-ALL when the blood and marrow are the primary sites and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma (T-LBL) when the primary site is a lymph node, the mediastinum (thymus) or another tissue such as the skin, tonsils, liver, spleen, CNS or testes. Again, no set blast number is required, with caution under 20 percent.

T-ALL typically brings a high white count, often with a large mediastinal mass; lymphadenopathy and an enlarged liver and spleen are common. T-LBL often presents as a rapidly growing anterior mediastinal mass, sometimes as a respiratory emergency. Its lymphoblasts are indistinguishable under the microscope from those of B-ALL: flow cytometry, showing T-lineage antigens, tells them apart. Long-term response rates approach 85 percent in children and adolescents and 60 percent in adults.

When acute leukemia comes from something else

He said some patients develop acute leukemia de novo, with no precursor lesion, but others first have a pre-neoplastic myeloid disorder, such as myelodysplastic syndrome, or CML, which can eventually become an acute leukemia. On his slide: acute leukemia, or a blast phase, can be the final stage of another marrow disorder, the result of treatment for a different cancer, or linked to a genetic disorder.

  • Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS): persistent cytopenias with abnormal function and look of the red cell, granulocyte and/or megakaryocyte precursors. It may start with few blasts and progress to more.
  • CML and CMML (chronic myelomonocytic leukemia).
  • The myeloproliferative neoplasms, with persistently high counts: polycythemia vera (increased red cells), essential thrombocythemia (increased platelets) and primary myelofibrosis (fibrosis in the marrow).
  • Myeloid neoplasm after cytotoxic therapy: after alkylating agents and/or ionizing radiation (type 1) or after topoisomerase II inhibitors (type 2). It generally arises within 10 years of the last exposure and has a bad prognosis.
  • Myeloid proliferations of Down syndrome: two clonal conditions of children with trisomy 21, transient abnormal myelopoiesis and myeloid leukemia of Down syndrome.

Treating acute leukemia

Treatment of acute leukemia has two objectives: eradicate the leukemic cell mass, with cytoreductive chemotherapy, radiotherapy and marrow transplant, and provide supportive care. The goal is complete remission: no leukemia-related signs or symptoms, no demonstrable disease, and the return of marrow function, with the blood's granulocyte, platelet and red cell values back to normal.

The translocations side by side

Five translocations run through this lecture, and they are easy to swap. These are the molecular associations he said you need: "You do need to know the molecular associations on the ones that are sort of underlined."

t(11;14)Cyclin D1 and IGHMantle cell lymphoma (at least 95 percent)Cyclin D1 on; the cyclin D1 stain is diagnostic
t(8;14)MYC and IGHBurkitt lymphoma (80 percent)MYC on: very fast growth

A memory hook: the three B-cell lymphomas all move a gene next to IGH on chromosome 14: BCL2 from 18 (follicular), cyclin D1 from 11 (mantle cell), MYC from 8 (Burkitt). The two myeloid ones are fusions: BCR with ABL1 in CML, PML with RARA in APL.

plain.dental:
What's tested
  • Which gland makes which hormone, and the three kinds of hormones
  • What each hormone problem looks like in the mouth and on the X-ray
  • What to do for these patients in the chair, especially diabetics: his numbers and how to fix low sugar
  • How to spot thyroid storm, adrenal crisis and low blood sugar
  • His three patient cases

Dr. Taylor's lecture is a review of the endocrine system for dentists. For each gland: what it makes, what goes wrong, and what you see in the mouth. Then three patients. These notes follow his recording and slides.

The basics

Hormones control growth, metabolism, reproduction, stress, calcium, and fluid balance. They travel in the blood, so they are slower than nerves, but they last longer and take longer to shut off.

Three kinds, and he said you need to know them: amine (epinephrine, norepinephrine), peptide (insulin), steroid (estrogen, testosterone). Peptides like insulin bind on the cell surface. Steroids go inside the cell, to the nucleus.

Negative feedback keeps hormones in range. When a gland's hormone gets low, the signal from the pituitary goes up.

Pituitary

The hypothalamus is the boss of the pituitary. The front of the pituitary makes ACTH for the adrenal cortex, TSH for the thyroid, GH for growth, FSH and LH for reproduction, and prolactin for milk. The back makes ADH, which saves water, and oxytocin. Too little ADH is diabetes insipidus: the kidneys dump water and the patient is always thirsty. That is not the sugar diabetes.

Growth hormone stays all your life. Sex hormones at puberty close the growth plates, so the long bones stop growing. Wait until a young patient has stopped growing before placing an implant, or the face grows around it.

Too much growth hormone before puberty makes a very tall person. After puberty it is acromegaly. Watch the jaw: it grows, the bite slides toward Class III, gaps open between the teeth, and the tongue gets big.

Thyroid

The thyroid makes T3 and T4, under TSH from the pituitary. They run metabolism and body heat. In thyroid surgery, the surgeon first finds the recurrent laryngeal nerve: damage it and the patient is left hoarse, usually for good.

Too much (hyperthyroid): weight loss, fast heart, always hot. Teeth come in early in kids. These patients are extra sensitive to epinephrine, so go easy on the vasoconstrictor if the disease isn't controlled.

Too little (hypothyroid), which you'll see far more often: tired, weight gain, slow heart. Teeth can come in late; more often you see a big tongue and slow healing.

Memory trick: hyper is fast, hypo is slow. Fast heart and early teeth, or slow heart and late teeth.

Thyroid storm is rare: the gland dumps a lot of hormone at once. High fever, a heart rate of 140 or more, agitated, shaky, nauseated, delirious, high blood pressure. It is life-threatening: call 911.

Calcium

PTH from the four parathyroids raises calcium fast. It makes bone break down (osteoclasts), makes the kidneys hold on to calcium, and has the kidneys make active vitamin D so the gut absorbs calcium.

Vitamin D is the slow, long-term controller. It is activated in the kidney.

Calcitonin comes from the thyroid when calcium is high. It undoes PTH.

Too much PTH: bone breaks down. On the X-ray you lose the lamina dura, the thin white line of bone around each root. You can get brown tumors, which look dark (radiolucent), and the teeth get loose. Send the patient to their doctor.

Too little PTH: calcium drops. Muscles twitch and lock up (tetany).

Adrenal glands

The outer part, the cortex, makes cortisol (stress, immune system, sugar) and aldosterone (keeps sodium, handles potassium). The inner part, the medulla, makes epinephrine and norepinephrine. That matters for the vasoconstrictor in your anesthetic and for keeping patients calm. Trick: a corticosteroid comes from the cortex.

Addison disease: not enough cortisol. Low blood pressure, tired, dark skin, and brown patches in the mouth. Why brown? Low cortisol lets ACTH climb, and ACTH turns on the pigment cells.

Adrenal crisis is Addison's emergency. It can be set off by a long or stressful surgery, a bad infection or injury, or a missed steroid dose. After a big procedure the patient may need extra steroid; ask their doctor how much. Look for very low blood pressure, weakness, confusion, passing out and shock.

Cushing syndrome: too much cortisol, and it looks just like long-term steroid pills. Round "moon" face, a hump between the shoulders, high blood sugar. In the mouth: more infections and slow healing.

Pancreas and diabetes

Alpha cells make glucagon, which breaks down stored sugar and makes new sugar. Beta cells make insulin, which moves sugar into cells and stores it.

Type 1: the immune system destroys the beta cells, so the patient needs insulin shots. Type 2: the body resists insulin, and insulin levels run high. The insulin is there but doesn't work.

His numbers: a finger-stick under 60 means give sugar. An HbA1c above 7 means poor control, with more implant failures and more gum disease. Below 7 is good control; most people without diabetes run about 5.

Metformin stops the liver from making sugar. A diabetic who took it and skipped breakfast can go low in your chair.

In the mouth, diabetes brings dry mouth, thrush (candidiasis), burning mouth, slow healing, more gum disease and more cavities. Saliva comes from the blood, so high blood sugar means sugary saliva that feeds yeast and cavity germs.

Gum disease and diabetes make each other worse. Keep the mouth clean.

Why extractions heal slowly: high sugar, weak immune cells (neutrophils), poor blood supply and poor collagen. So expect slow healing and infection.

The diabetic patient in your chair

Before: check how well the sugar is controlled (HbA1c). Ask if they ate and took their medicine. Book mornings.

During: watch for low sugar: sweating, shaking, confusion, a fast heart. Check a finger-stick (ask first). A glucose monitor on the arm may not read very low numbers, so check anyway.

If they're awake, give straight glucose. Table sugar is half fructose, which the liver has to convert first, so glucose works faster. Drugs like Mounjaro slow the stomach, so sugar by mouth works slowly. If it fails: IV sugar, or a glucagon shot. If they pass out, activate emergency protocols.

Low sugar or thyroid storm? Both shake and race. Fever and high blood pressure mean thyroid storm.

Sex hormones

Puberty: gums get more inflamed. Pregnancy: more estrogen and progesterone, so pregnancy gingivitis and the pyogenic granuloma, the "pregnancy tumor," a lump of gum tissue usually between two teeth. Menopause: dry mouth, changed taste, and weaker bones.

His three patients

Lucilla, Graves disease, heart racing, pulse 112: the thyroid is overactive, T3 and T4 are high. Go easy on epinephrine. Look for early eruption in the young, cavities, burning mouth, and a tremor that gets in the way. The danger is thyroid storm: check her heart rate first.

Proximo, type 2 diabetic for 22 years, skips his metformin, glucose 220, HbA1c 9.8 percent, needs extractions, smokes a pack a day: the problem is insulin that doesn't work. Expect slow healing, check his control first, and time the visit after his meal and medicine. Pack-years are packs a day times years: a pack a day for 40 years is 40 pack-years.

Commodus, Addison disease, brown patches in the mouth, blood pressure 90 over 60: the adrenal cortex is failing and cortisol is low. High ACTH causes the brown color. Long surgery, infection or a missed steroid dose can set off an adrenal crisis, and he may need extra steroid after a big procedure.
plain.preg:
What's tested
  • hCG: where it comes from, how it saves the corpus luteum, and that a pregnancy test measures it
  • Milk: prolactin makes it, oxytocin lets it down, progesterone holds it back until delivery, dopamine keeps prolactin low, and prolactin stops periods
  • How a sperm gets into the egg: ZP3, ZP2, and the block on a second sperm; and capacitation first
  • Where the pregnancy hormones come from: estriol needs the baby's help, progesterone doesn't
  • Implantation, the placenta's other hormones (hPL and relaxin), and what starts labor

Dr. Madison's lecture follows a pregnancy from start to finish, with the focus on hormones: getting sperm and egg together, implantation, the placenta and its hormones, labor, breastfeeding and birth control. These notes follow his recording and slides.

A quick review of the cycle

After ovulation, the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum. It makes progesterone, the key hormone that gets the uterine lining ready for an embryo: wider vessels and stored sugar (glycogen). If there's no pregnancy, the corpus luteum dies after about 14 days, becomes a scar called the corpus albicans, the hormones crash, and the lining is shed.

Getting sperm to the egg

About 250 million sperm go in, and only about 50 reach the far end of the fallopian tube, where the egg is usually fertilized. Sperm can fertilize for 24 to 48 hours.

At ovulation estrogen is in charge, and it helps the sperm three ways: it buffers the vaginal pH (makes it less acidic), it thins the cervical mucus, and it makes the uterine muscle (the myometrium) contract to push sperm upward.

The egg's three layers

From the outside in: the cumulus cells (he called them the corona radiata), the zona pellucida (a thick capsule), and the egg's own membrane. The sperm's acrosome, a cap full of enzymes, digests its way through.

Fertilization

The sperm first binds ZP3 on the zona, and that sets off the acrosomal reaction: the acrosome bursts and releases its enzymes. ZP3 is cleaved away, and the sperm binds ZP2 next. Then the egg finishes its second meiotic division (the first was at ovulation), and the cortical reaction sheds the rest of the zona proteins so no other sperm can get in. One sperm, one egg. The two pronuclei fuse, and you have a zygote.

Memory trick: ZP3 comes first, as in "3, 2, go."

Capacitation

Fresh sperm can't fertilize yet. In the male tract, cholesterol keeps their membrane stiff so the acrosome can't burst early. In the female tract they lose that cholesterol, calcium can get in, blocking proteins are removed, and the tail switches from a wave to a whip. Now the acrosomal reaction can happen.

The fallopian tubes

The finger-like fimbriae catch the egg. Cilia and muscle contractions move it along. Fertilization usually happens in the far (distal) part of the tube.

Estrogen holds back, progesterone lets in

Right after ovulation estrogen is still high, and it squeezes the opening into the uterus, holding the embryo back while the lining gets ready. When progesterone rises, the muscle relaxes and the embryo moves in. Remember: estrogen contracts, progesterone relaxes.

The first week

Fertilization happens within a day of ovulation. The embryo reaches the uterus about 4 days after ovulation and implants 5 to 7 days after. About 8 days after ovulation it starts making hCG.

The blastocyst

The embryo implants as a blastocyst: a ball of cells with a fluid-filled space. Its outer layer is the trophoblasts, the cells that do the implanting. He said you don't need the names of the earlier stages.

Implantation

The blastocyst puts out sticky adhesion molecules, enzymes (proteases) and hormones (hCG). The lining gets ready too, which is called decidualization: more blood vessels, more glycogen, and a calmer local immune system so the embryo isn't attacked as foreign.

When it sticks, the trophoblasts split into two kinds. Cytotrophoblasts are the nurse cells. Syncytiotrophoblasts are the invaders: they push enzymes into the lining to dig in, and they make hormones (hCG and hPL). With progesterone's help, the lining cells swell with glycogen and become decidual cells that feed the embryo until the placenta is ready.

hCG saves the corpus luteum

hCG comes from the trophoblasts. It tells the corpus luteum "we're pregnant," so it doesn't die. The corpus luteum keeps making progesterone and estrogen, even more than before. LH and FSH stay low, so there are no more cycles and no periods.

A pregnancy test measures hCG. It shows up in urine or blood about 10 to 11 days after fertilization and peaks around 10 weeks.

Side notes from his slides: hCG can weakly turn on the thyroid's TSH receptor, causing a short-lived overactive thyroid. Estrogen raises the thyroid's carrier protein, so total thyroid hormone goes up but free hormone barely changes.

Corpus luteum, then placenta

The corpus luteum makes most of the progesterone and estrogen for the first trimester. The placenta starts growing after implantation, is finished by the end of the first trimester, and takes over.

The placenta

It trades gases and food, makes hormones, protects the baby from many infections while letting the mother's antibodies through, and sends the baby's waste back to the mother. Oxygen, water and nutrients go to the baby; carbon dioxide and waste come back. Some drugs and viruses get through too.

hPL

Human placental lactogen, also called human chorionic somatomammotropin, helps the breasts develop. It also works against insulin: it breaks down fat, sugar and protein to keep fuel flowing to the baby. So pregnancy is insulin resistant, with high insulin levels, and some mothers get gestational diabetes. It has many causes, genes included.

Relaxin

Made by the corpus luteum (because of hCG) and the placenta. It keeps the uterus quiet so the baby doesn't come early, loosens the pelvic ligaments and softens the cervix.

Making the pregnancy hormones

It all starts with the mother's cholesterol. The placenta makes progesterone by itself.

Estrogen needs teamwork. The main estrogen of pregnancy is estriol (estradiol is the normal cycle's, estrone is menopause's). The placenta is missing one enzyme, 17,20 desmolase, so it hands the job to the baby. The baby's adrenal gland makes DHEA sulfate, the baby's liver changes it, and the placenta's aromatase turns it into estriol. That's why the mother's estriol shows how healthy the baby is.

Labor

Labor comes about 40 weeks after the last period started. The baby stretches the uterus. The uterus makes more receptors for oxytocin and the prostaglandin PGF2 alpha. The balance tips toward estrogen, so the muscle contracts. Prostaglandins raise calcium in the muscle for stronger contractions, and PGE2 softens the cervix. Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary is the big one: it drives contractions, and more contractions bring more oxytocin. After birth, oxytocin keeps the uterus contracting, which stops heavy bleeding.

Getting the breast ready

During pregnancy, estrogen grows the ducts and adds fat, progesterone adds alveoli (the milk-making sacs), and prolactin and cortisol build up the milk-making enzymes. But progesterone blocks prolactin, so full milk waits for delivery.

After delivery

Progesterone drops when the placenta comes out, and prolactin is free to make milk. Oxytocin squeezes the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli, and the milk comes out (letdown). Prolactin makes it, oxytocin lets it down.

Controlling prolactin and oxytocin

Normally the brain keeps prolactin low with dopamine. Suckling lowers dopamine, so prolactin rises. Suckling also releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary. High prolactin blocks GnRH, so LH and FSH fall and periods stop. That's why breastfeeding mothers often have no periods. He said to focus on dopamine.

Birth control

Three ways. Stop ovulation: the pill, whose estrogen blocks the LH surge (it also thins the lining and thickens mucus). Keep sperm and egg apart: barriers and others he skipped. Stop implantation: high-dose estrogen (a lining that grows but never gets progesterone's preparation), the IUD, or drugs that block progesterone's receptor. Progestin makes the cervical mucus thick so sperm can't get in.
plain.sexster:
What's tested
  • The drug names in each class, especially the ones he highlighted in red
  • What 5-alpha-reductase and aromatase do to testosterone, and the drugs that block them
  • Blood clots: the biggest risk of estrogens, shared by the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors
  • The three ways to block androgens
  • Tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for bone, Clomid for ovulation
  • Testosterone's liver risk, and Plan B versus ulipristal

Dr. Fasinu's drug lecture on the sex hormones: androgens and the drugs that block them, estrogens and the drugs that block them, then progestins and anti-progestins. He said to focus on the drugs he highlighted on his slides. These notes follow the recording and slides.

Which hormone to avoid

Avoid testosterone with an enlarged prostate (BPH), in pregnancy and in a man with breast cancer. Avoid estrogen with breast cancer and in anyone who has had a blood clot. Clots are estrogen's worst and most common side effect.

Making the hormones

Cholesterol becomes DHEA, then androstenedione, then testosterone. DHEA is sold over the counter as a supplement, and older men take it for "andropause." Every other testosterone product is a controlled drug (Schedule III). His slide's table calls DHEA "dihydrotestosterone"; he corrected it: DHEA is dehydroepiandrosterone, and DHT is dihydrotestosterone.

Testosterone then goes one of two ways. 5-alpha-reductase turns it into DHT, the active form. Aromatase turns it into estradiol. Block the first and you lower androgen activity; block the second and you lower estrogen.

DHT makes you grow; estradiol stops growth by closing the growth plates. A man with no aromatase has no estradiol, so he grows very tall with weak, thin bones.

Testosterone

The hypothalamus sends GnRH in pulses, the pituitary answers with LH and FSH, and the testes make testosterone. Testosterone makes more red blood cells, holds on to salt and water (bad for high blood pressure), lowers good cholesterol (HDL), builds muscle, and lowers the proteins that carry hormones in the blood. Like all steroid hormones, it rides a carrier (SHBG), gets into the cell and works on the genes, so it is slow.

Drugs: testosterone itself (gel, patch, nasal gel, injection) and testosterone cypionate, the shot into the muscle that lasts for weeks. Know those two; he didn't want to bother you with the others on his table. Uses: low testosterone in men, anemia that won't respond to other treatment, muscle wasting, and aging men.

Side effects are worse in women and children. Women grow facial hair and get a deep voice, an enlarged clitoris and smaller breasts, sometimes for good. Men can get sleep apnea, a painful lasting erection (priapism) and breast growth, probably because some testosterone turns into estradiol. The one he said to remember: liver damage. No testosterone with liver disease or in pregnancy. Put the gel on at bedtime so you don't pass it to a child by hugging.

Blocking androgens: three ways

  • GnRH analogs (goserelin, sold as Zoladex; leuprolide): natural GnRH comes in pulses. A long-acting copy that never stops switches the pituitary off, so testosterone falls. Used for prostate cancer, BPH, early puberty and chemical castration. Side effects: impotence and breast growth.
  • 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride): they stop testosterone from becoming DHT. Proscar and Propecia are both finasteride: the bigger dose for BPH, the smaller one for hair loss. Side effects: breast growth and sexual problems.
  • Androgen receptor blockers (flutamide, bicalutamide): they sit on the androgen receptor. Used for prostate cancer, and for too much androgen in women. Side effects: stomach upset (least with bicalutamide), breast growth and liver damage.

Estrogens

There are three natural ones: estradiol from the ovary, and estrone and estriol from the liver and other tissues. Estrone and estriol leave in the bile and come back from the gut. Estrogen taken by mouth hits the liver hardest.

Estrogen builds the female body and the uterine lining, raises good cholesterol (and triglycerides), protects bone and keeps skin healthy (some teens get the pill for their skin). It also makes the liver produce more clotting factors (2, 7, 9 and 10) and less antithrombin III. That is why estrogens, and even the anti-estrogens, cause clots.

Drugs: estradiol (patch, gel, shot); ethinyl estradiol, the one in birth control pills; and estrone, the main part of Premarin, for menopause. Uses: low estrogen, menopause, birth control, very painful periods or excess hair, and fertility.

Side effects: nausea, fluid retention (an androgen problem too; it raises blood pressure), breakthrough bleeding and sore breasts; and the serious ones, clots, uterine and breast cancer, and high blood pressure. Adding progesterone protects the uterus. No estrogen in pregnancy, in someone still growing, with unexplained genital bleeding, after any clot or stroke (even 10 years ago), with heart disease, or with a family history of breast or uterine cancer. Estrogen also makes blood thinners like warfarin work less well.

SERMs

Estrogen has two receptors, alpha and beta, and each tissue has its own mix. So one drug can act like estrogen in one tissue and block it in another.

  • Tamoxifen: blocks estrogen in the breast and turns it on in the uterus. For breast cancer, but only when the tumor has estrogen receptors. Risks: uterine cancer and clots.
  • Raloxifene (Evista): for bone loss after menopause. It doesn't stimulate the uterus or the breast. Clot risk is 2 to 3 times higher.
  • Clomiphene (Clomid): blocks estrogen's brake on the brain, so LH and FSH surge and the ovary releases eggs. A fertility drug; twins and triplets are common.

His short version: tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for osteoporosis, Clomid for ovulation.

Aromatase inhibitors

Anastrozole (Arimidex) stops testosterone from becoming estradiol, to treat breast cancer. Remember hot flashes and clots. Not for women before menopause or with liver damage.

Progesterone and progestins

Progesterone matures the uterine lining. Progestin drugs act on its receptor and hold down FSH, so no egg is released. Women who can't take estrogen (a clot, or breast or uterine cancer) use progestin-only birth control. Levonorgestrel is the common one, and Plan B is a big dose of it. Side effects: high blood pressure and lower HDL.

His cases

Least estrogen-like of four hormones: levonorgestrel, a progestin. A man on finasteride for hair loss with a low sex drive and sore breasts: the drug blocks 5-alpha-reductase. A woman on raloxifene whose extraction site heals slowly: watch for a clot while she's laid up.

Emergency contraception

Plan B (levonorgestrel) works within 72 hours and needs no prescription. Ulipristal (Ella) blocks the progesterone receptor, works up to 5 days, and needs a prescription. Mifepristone also blocks cortisol's receptor, so it is not for someone with Addison disease.
plain.hemeintro:
What's tested
  • The white cells: two classes and five types, how to tell them apart and what each one does; and platelets come from megakaryocytes
  • B cells (antibodies, plasma cells), the two kinds of T cells, and NK cells, including how MHC class I keeps an NK cell from killing a healthy cell
  • Innate versus adaptive immunity
  • Primary organs (just the bone marrow and the thymus) versus secondary ones, and the thymus's special framework of epithelioreticular cells
  • The thymus, the lymph node and the spleen: their parts and what happens in each; for the spleen, "associate this PALS with the spleen"
  • He said he won't ask about stained images or the typical cell counts

Dr. Herr's Lecture 19, a short one on Tuesday, November 17, started the blood part of the course: first the blood cells, then the organs where immune cells grow up and go to work. These notes follow the recording and slides.

The cells of the blood

Red cells are most of the cells in blood (about 99 percent) and carry oxygen and carbon dioxide. Platelets are pieces of big bone marrow cells called megakaryocytes, and they start clotting; he called that "just knowledge you should know." White cells come in two classes and five types: the granulocytes, with obvious granules (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils), and the agranulocytes, without them (monocytes and lymphocytes).

Most to least common: neutrophils (50 to 70 percent), lymphocytes (30 to 40), monocytes (2 to 8), eosinophils (1 to 4), basophils (under 1). Memory trick: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas. He said there's no reason to memorize the cells' typical counts in the blood: learn their names and jobs.

Where the blood cells come from

One stem cell splits into two lines. The lymphoid line makes the B and T cells. The myeloid line stays in the bone marrow and makes the red cells, the megakaryocytes (platelets), the granulocytes and the monocytes. In adults, every blood cell starts in the bone marrow.

Innate and adaptive immunity

Innate immunity is already there before any germ shows up, and it isn't aimed at anything in particular: skin and mucous membranes, acid, lysozyme, thiocyanate in saliva, interferons, the eating cells (neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages) and NK cells.

Adaptive immunity starts after the body meets a specific antigen, and it often remembers it. B cells make antibodies (the humoral arm), and T cells attack infected and cancerous cells (the cellular arm), and the two work together. His shortcut: hear "humoral," think B cells and antibodies.

The white cells one by one

Neutrophil: a nucleus with several lobes, two kinds of granules (the first kind holds elastase and myeloperoxidase), and stored glycogen. The main eating cell in the blood and the first defense against bacteria. It stays in the blood about 10 hours.

Eosinophil: a two-lobed nucleus and big granules that stain red. Its major basic protein punches holes in parasites. It goes up with parasites and allergies like hay fever, and it has IgE receptors.

Basophil: the rarest, under 1 percent. A two-lobed nucleus and dark blue to purple granules full of heparin and histamine. It has IgE receptors and plays a big part in asthma.

Monocyte: a big cell with a horseshoe-shaped nucleus. It stays in the blood about 3 days, then moves into tissue and becomes a macrophage. It eats bacteria and debris and has MHC II.

Lymphocyte: a round nucleus with just a thin rim of pale cytoplasm. Small ones are B and T cells; large ones are NK cells.

B cells, T cells and NK cells

B cells wear IgM and IgD on their surface as antigen sensors. When a B cell's antibody fits an antigen, it calls in helper T cells and turns into a plasma cell, in a secondary lymphoid organ, that pours out copies of that antibody. Plasma cell means antibody production.

T cells use a T cell receptor, and they only see antigen that another cell holds up on MHC. In his words, helper T cells help the B cells, and cytotoxic T cells kill whatever they bind. Helper T cells are CD4 and read MHC II on cells like macrophages; they send out signals that boost B, T and NK cells. Cytotoxic T cells are CD8 and read MHC I; they kill infected cells with perforins and help reject transplants and fight tumors. Trick: 4 times 2 is 8, 8 times 1 is 8.

NK cells have no B or T markers and no antigen-specific receptor. They kill virus-infected and tumor cells. Their CD16 grabs the tail end of IgG, so they can kill a cell that antibodies have tagged. That is ADCC, and macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils can do it too, with perforins, granzymes, TNF and enzymes.

How an NK cell decides: it has an activating receptor and an inhibitory receptor. A healthy cell shows MHC class I, which the inhibitory receptor binds, so the NK cell leaves it alone. A tumor or virus-infected cell that has lost its MHC class I gets killed. And a cell with far too many activating signals can get killed even with its MHC class I, which may play a part in autoimmunity.

What the lymphoid organs do

They find and get rid of germs, foreign material, transplanted cells and cancer cells. Primary organs, just the bone marrow and the thymus for this class (not GALT, he said), raise the B and T cells without any antigen around. Bone marrow, B cells; thymus, T cells. Any other lymphoid organ is secondary. Secondary organs (lymph nodes, the gut and throat lymphoid tissue, and the spleen) are where those cells meet antigen and get activated.

Every lymphoid organ is built on a frame of reticular cells and type III collagen, except the thymus, whose frame is epithelioreticular cells. He said, "I do want you to know that."

The bone marrow

B cells and NK cells are born and grow up in the marrow, and B cells that attack the body's own tissue are removed there. T cell precursors start in the marrow but go to the thymus to finish.

The thymus

It sits behind the top of the breastbone. It is biggest in babies and children, then by the teens it shrinks and turns to fat: in an adult donor, the fat in front of the heart is the old thymus. It has lymphatics going out but none coming in. Its T cell receptors get their variety by rearranging genes, and 95 to 99 percent of the T cells in it die.

Its outer cortex is dark, packed with young T cells, and macrophages eat the ones that fail. Its inner medulla is lighter, with fewer, bigger T cells and Hassall's corpuscles, little onion-like balls of flat cells. The blood-thymus barrier (capillary wall and basement membrane, macrophages, epithelioreticular cells) keeps antigens away from the young T cells.

T cell school: precursors come in through postcapillary venules, pass a first test in the cortex (positive selection) and a second in the medulla (negative selection, which removes cells that attack self), and leave as either CD4 or CD8 cells.

Secondary organs

Lymph nodes filter lymph, the gut and throat tissue guard the linings, and the spleen filters blood.

Lymphatic vessels

They start as dead-end tubes in connective tissue that soak up fluid, antigens and cells, run through lymph nodes, and empty into the subclavian veins through the thoracic duct.

Lymph nodes

Small bean-shaped organs with a capsule. B cells sit in the outer cortex, in follicles; T cells sit in the paracortex below it. A resting follicle is just a ball of B cells; after antigen arrives it grows a germinal center, where B cells multiply, with a mantle around it.

Lymph comes in through afferent vessels, runs through the sinus under the capsule and the sinuses beside the trabeculae, and leaves through an efferent one: the lymph node is the only lymphoid organ with both. Lymphocytes from the blood get in through high endothelial venules. Nodes make mostly IgG.

An antigen's trip, region by region: in through the afferent vessel, the first T and B cell activation in the paracortex, B cell activation in a primary follicle, B cells multiplying and maturing in a germinal center, plasma cells making antibody in the medulla, and out the efferent vessel.

Dendritic cells show antigen to T cells. Follicular dendritic cells hold antigen for B cells in germinal centers but can't present it, because they have no MHC II.

Gut lymphoid tissue and the tonsils

MALT is loose lymphoid tissue under the linings of the gut, airways and urinary and genital tracts. Its nodules are mostly B cells, with T cells around them, and it makes IgA that is pumped into the lumen. Peyer's patches are clumps of it in the ileum, and M cells on top of them carry antigens in from the gut.

The tonsils ring the back of the mouth and nose (Waldeyer's ring): the pharyngeal tonsil at the back of the nasal cavity, the tubal tonsils where the auditory tube opens, the palatine tonsils at the back of the throat, and the lingual tonsils on the back of the tongue. They catch what you breathe and eat, and the palatine tonsils' crypts trap material so there's more time to respond. They have no incoming lymphatics. A child's swollen, inflamed pharyngeal tonsil (the adenoid) is adenoiditis and can block breathing.

The spleen

The biggest lymphoid organ, in the upper left belly. Blood and its antigens come in by the splenic artery, off the celiac trunk. It filters blood, not lymph, so it has no incoming lymphatics. It removes old red cells and platelets, recycles iron, holds about a third of the platelets, and makes IgM and IgG.

Its tissue is white pulp and red pulp. White pulp is lymphoid tissue around a central arteriole: T cells hug the arteriole (the PALS, which he said to associate with the spleen), B cells sit in nodules beside it, and a marginal zone of macrophages and some B cells wraps around it. Red pulp, most of the spleen, is splenic cords and sinuses.

In the open circulation, blood from the sheathed capillaries spills into the cords, macrophages check it, and the cells squeeze back into the sinuses through slits between rod-shaped lining cells. The sinus wall has only hoops of basal lamina, and no muscle or pericytes.

Where the B and T cells are

B cells: lymph node follicles, spleen nodules, gut nodules. T cells: lymph node paracortex, the spleen's PALS, the areas around the gut nodules, and the thymus.
plain.lymleuk:
What's tested
  • The five translocations he said you need: t(14;18) follicular, t(11;14) mantle cell (a cyclin D1 stain means mantle cell), t(8;14) Burkitt, t(9;22) CML, t(15;17) APL
  • Which lymphomas are B-cell and which T-cell, which are slow and which fast, and Hodgkin versus the rest
  • Acute leukemia: blasts, more than 20 percent; Auer rods mean myeloid; AML in adults, ALL in children; APL (bleeding, a great cure) and acute monocytic leukemia in the gums
  • CML, the chronic leukemia to know, and CLL with its smudge cells
  • The B symptoms, and what these diseases look like in the mouth

Dr. Borak's lecture on Tuesday, November 17, covers the blood cancers: lymphomas, which start in the lymph system, and leukemias, which start in the marrow. He said not to freak out about the amount of detail: know the basics, each disease's category and its translocation. You don't need the CD markers or the flow cytometry details. These notes follow the recording and slides.

How blood cells mature

Every blood cell comes from a stem cell in the marrow, down a myeloid line (red cells, platelets, neutrophils, monocytes) or a lymphoid line (B, T and NK cells). Mostly the white cells turn cancerous: the myeloid ones mostly into leukemias, the lymphoid ones into lymphomas or leukemias. A neutrophil grows up in this order: myeloblast, promyelocyte (granules appear), myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, segmented neutrophil. The blast is the youngest. In leukemia the cells get stuck young, and blasts pile up. Blasts in the blood are never normal, except in a newborn.

What a lymphoma is

A lymphoma is a cancer of lymphocytes, and it can start in lymph tissue almost anywhere. You need a piece of tissue, a node or marrow, to diagnose it; he likes to take out the whole node. Big nodes aren't always lymphoma: infections and diseases like lupus swell them too.

The B symptoms

He called them high-yield clues: a fever of 38 degrees Celsius or more, night sweats that soak the sheets, and losing at least 10 percent of your weight in 6 months without trying. Tuberculosis can do this too, so you still need the tissue.

The tissue and flow cytometry

A normal node is rubbery, with follicles in its outer layer and open channels (sinuses). A lymphoma node is fleshy, and its normal pattern is wiped out by one kind of cell. The lab looks at the cells (the H and E stain), stains the tissue with antibodies, and runs flow cytometry, which tells B cell, T cell or myeloid, young or mature. Each B cell carries kappa or lambda; a normal node has both, but a lymphoma's cells all carry just one, because they are one clone. Send the tissue for flow fresh, not in formalin, in a medium like RPMI or Hanks's solution, because flow needs living cells. Flow shines a laser through cells one at a time: forward scatter tells the size, side scatter tells how grainy the cell is. He said not to spend a second on the CD markers.

Classifying lymphoma

It takes everything together, but how the cells look matters most. Most lymphomas, 85 to 90 percent, are B-cell. Most of the rest are T-cell; NK-cell ones are rare. Each comes from a normal cell: the follicle's center gives follicular lymphoma, the rim around it (the mantle) gives mantle cell lymphoma, and the zone outside that gives marginal zone lymphoma.

Lymphoma near the mouth and eye

Lymphoma can start in the eye (painless blurry vision or floaters, or a puffy, salmon-colored swelling beside the eye), the tonsils (very swollen), and the gums (a flat or ulcerated patch rather than a lump).

Hodgkin versus the rest

Hodgkin lymphoma is usually found in one area. It starts in nodes deep in the chest, spreads node to node in order, rarely leaves the nodes and never gets into the blood, and its cancer cells are a few big, odd-looking cells. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is usually widespread when found, can skip nodes, often starts outside them, can get into the blood, and its cells look like normal lymphocytes. They are treated differently.

Staging

Staging asks how far it has spread: one place or several, above the diaphragm, below it or both, outside the nodes, or everywhere. Everywhere is stage 4, the worst. B means B symptoms.

What leukemia is

Lymphoma is mostly in nodes; leukemia is mostly in the marrow and blood. Leukemia is cancer cells taking over the marrow and blood. It starts in the marrow and can spread to the spleen, liver and nodes. Untreated, it kills. It hurts you two ways. The marrow fails: anemia (tired, pale), low platelets (bruising, bleeding) and too few good white cells (fever, infections). And the cells move into organs: bone pain, a big spleen and liver, big nodes, nerve problems, and swollen gums. He said a dentist may be the first to spot a leukemia this way.

The marrow exam

A blood count flags the blasts, a smear confirms them, then the marrow is sampled, numbed first. The back of the hip bone (posterior iliac crest) gives both a core biopsy and an aspirate. The sternum gives an aspirate only (the heart is right under it), and so does the tibia in small children.

Acute versus chronic

Acute: blasts over 20 percent, a fast start, death in under 6 months without treatment, very low platelets, mildly enlarged organs. Chronic myeloid: mature cells, under 20 percent blasts, a slow start, 2 to 6 years without treatment, platelets normal or high at first, a big spleen. Both kill by infection or bleeding.

AML and ALL

He said acute leukemia is mostly children for ALL, but adults for AML (median age 65). ALL is mostly in small children, usually 1 to 5, and does badly under age 1. Myeloblasts are bigger, with granules and sometimes Auer rods. Lymphoblasts are smaller, with little cytoplasm and no granules. An Auer rod means it isn't ALL.

The number: more than 20 percent blasts makes the diagnosis. If the AML has one of its defining genetic changes, the blast count doesn't matter. You don't need the AML subtypes.

Indolent or aggressive

He wants you to know each lymphoma's group. Slow B-cell: CLL/SLL, follicular, mantle cell, marginal zone. Fast B-cell: diffuse large B-cell, Burkitt. T-cell: mycosis fungoides (slow), Sézary syndrome, peripheral T-cell and NK/T-cell lymphoma (fast). Hodgkin and the plasma cell tumors are groups of their own.

CLL/SLL

Small, mature B cells in older people (median 70 or older). Called CLL when there are at least 5,000 per microliter of these B cells in the blood, SLL when it is mostly in the nodes. Same disease. Fewer than that, with no node disease, is a pre-cancer called monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis. On the smear: "soccer ball" chromatin and smudge cells. Infections come from low antibodies. It is slow but mostly incurable.

Follicular lymphoma

Crowded, back-to-back follicles. The translocation t(14;18) keeps BCL2 on, so the cells don't die. Usually widespread when found, but often without symptoms. Slow: median survival over 17 years.

Mantle cell lymphoma

From the mantle zone around the follicle. Small to medium cells with irregular nuclei and the translocation t(11;14), which nothing else has. He said if a question says the cells stain for cyclin D1, it's mantle cell lymphoma. Older patients (median 68 to 69) with big nodes. Survival has gotten much better.

MALT lymphoma

The one dentists will see most, he said: a slow B-cell lymphoma, often outside the nodes, grown out of long inflammation, with tumor cells invading the gland's lining. The stomach with H. pylori, the skin with Borrelia, the eye area with Chlamydia psittaci, the salivary gland after Sjögren syndrome, the thyroid after Hashimoto thyroiditis. Some respond to antibiotics.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Big B cells in sheets: about 30 percent of adult lymphomas. A node or mass that grows fast; 30 to 40 percent start outside the nodes (stomach, salivary glands, thyroid, bone). It grows fast, can start on its own or grow out of a slow lymphoma, and often brings B symptoms. About 70 percent are doing well at 5 years after R-CHOP.

Burkitt lymphoma

Very fast-growing B cells. The translocation t(8;14) turns on MYC. Under the microscope: a starry sky, pale macrophages eating dead tumor cells among blue tumor cells. The starry sky is the key finding. Endemic (equatorial Africa, Papua New Guinea): children, the jaws, EBV in over 90 percent. Sporadic (everywhere else): the abdomen, gums and tonsils, EBV in about 20 percent. (Once, aloud, he swapped the two names; his slide and the textbooks say it this way.) Also seen with HIV. Jaw pain and loose teeth can be the first sign. Treatment works very well: about 90 percent of children survive.

Hodgkin lymphoma

A few big Reed-Sternberg cells ("owl's eyes") in a crowd of normal immune cells: he said they are the main thing to recognize. It stays in nodes above the diaphragm (the neck, above the collarbone, the chest) and spreads node to node in order. Painless, firm nodes; rarely, node pain after alcohol. Starting outside the nodes is rare. Nodular sclerosis has bands of scar tissue; you don't need the differences between the types. EBV drives some cases. Over 80 percent are cured. The other lymphomas (non-Hodgkin) more often start outside the nodes and are more often widespread when found.

Plasma cell tumors

A plasmacytoma is one tumor of plasma cells, often in a rib or the spine. Multiple myeloma is plasma cells all through the marrow, making one antibody (the M-spike), with organ damage: CRAB, for high calcium, kidney damage, anemia and holes in the bones. Red cells stack like coins (rouleaux) because of all that antibody. Myeloma is usually incurable.

T-cell lymphoma

He skipped peripheral T-cell lymphoma, saying only: very aggressive, B symptoms, and chemotherapy often doesn't work.

Mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome

He went through these quickly. Mycosis fungoides is the most common lymphoma of the skin, and slow: skin patches, then plaques, then tumors, often in the "bathing trunk" area. Sézary syndrome: red skin all over, big nodes and the same cells (with brain-shaped nuclei) in the blood; aggressive.

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma

It starts in the nose, destroys vessels and tissue, and can punch a hole in the hard palate. Strongly linked to EBV; mostly in eastern Asia and Indigenous peoples of Central and South America.

CML

The chronic leukemia he said you need. The Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), makes BCR-ABL1, an enzyme stuck on. Most people are found in the slow chronic phase, sometimes by a routine blood count. The white count is very high (median about 80,000 per microliter), mostly neutrophils of every age, not blasts, and the spleen is big. Untreated, it turns into a blast phase in a few years. Imatinib (Gleevec) blocks the enzyme by taking ATP's place.

Blasts and Auer rods

Blasts mean acute leukemia, but a few (under 20 percent) can show up in MDS too. After the newborn period, any blast in the blood is abnormal. Auer rods are red-blue needles inside myeloblasts: an Auer rod means the blast is myeloid, never ALL.

APL

One of the two acute leukemias he said you need. A type of AML where the cells get stuck as promyelocytes, full of big granules and bundles of Auer rods. The translocation t(15;17) joins PML and RARA. The danger is DIC, clotting and bleeding all at once: bleeding gums, bruises, and early death. Retinoic acid with arsenic cures most.

Acute monocytic leukemia

The other acute leukemia he said you need, for one reason: it can show up in the mouth. An AML of monocyte-like cells with kidney-shaped nuclei. It can grow in the gums (myeloid sarcoma) and make them swell. Swollen gums in someone tired, pale and bruising: get a blood count.

B-ALL and T-ALL

For these he said you only need who gets them. B-ALL is the most common leukemia in children (75 percent are under 6), with a smaller second peak in the 40s. It shows as marrow failure. Over 90 percent of children do well. T-ALL looks the same under the microscope (tests show the T cells), and does a little worse; it often has a high white count and a mass in the chest, and the lymphoma form can block the airway.

Where acute leukemia comes from

Some acute leukemias start on their own. Others are the end of another marrow disease (MDS, CML, CMML, or a myeloproliferative neoplasm: polycythemia vera with too many red cells, essential thrombocythemia with too many platelets, myelofibrosis with a scarred marrow). It can come within 10 years of chemotherapy or radiation for another cancer, with a bad prognosis. And it can come with Down syndrome.

Treatment

Kill the leukemia (chemotherapy, radiation, transplant) and support the patient. The goal is complete remission: no symptoms, no disease found, normal blood counts.

The translocations

He said you do need these.

TranslocationDisease
t(14;18), BCL2Follicular lymphoma
t(11;14), cyclin D1Mantle cell lymphoma
t(8;14), MYCBurkitt lymphoma
t(9;22), BCR-ABL1 (Philadelphia)CML
t(15;17), PML-RARAAPL

In the mouth

Swollen gums: AML in the gums. Bleeding gums and spots: low platelets, or DIC in APL. A fast jaw mass in a child: Burkitt. A hole in the palate: NK/T-cell lymphoma. A new parotid lump with Sjögren: MALT lymphoma. Punched-out holes in the jaw with high calcium: myeloma.

What's tested
  • The major glands and their hormones, and the three hormone classes with an example of each ("you'll need to know that there's 3 main types of hormones")
  • The oral findings of each disorder: acromegaly's growing jaw, hyper- and hypothyroidism, hyper- and hypoparathyroidism on the radiograph, Addison disease, Cushing syndrome, diabetes, and puberty, pregnancy and menopause
  • His clinical points: implants wait until growth stops, the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery, epinephrine in hyperthyroidism, extra steroid after a big procedure in Addison disease

  • If a patient looks hypoglycemic, check a finger-stick even when the CGM shows a number: his patient's read 53 while she was in the 30s.

Two warnings from a patient of his. Some patients wear a continuous glucose monitor, or CGM, a sensor taped to the arm. Some CGMs only read down to a certain level: his patient's stopped at 53, and her finger-stick was in the 30s. It took 10 or 12 packets of glucose gel to bring her back. Not all sugars are the same. Table sugar, sucrose, is half glucose and half fructose, and the body can't use fructose (or galactose) directly: the liver has to convert it to glucose first. Straight glucose needs less processing, so it raises the blood sugar faster.

Thyroid storm, also called thyroid crisis or thyrotoxic crisis, is rare, but it happens: the gland releases a large amount of hormone in a short time. It is a life-threatening emergency. Growth hormone stays with you for life, but it is strongest in childhood and adolescence. What stops the long bones from growing is the sex hormones: at puberty the growth plates fuse, and growth hormone no longer lengthens them. He uses this in treatment planning. A 13- or 14-year-old boy who is growing hair on his upper lip is probably close to puberty and near his final height. If a patient lost a tooth at 10, he waits for growth to stop before placing an implant: an implant is fixed in the bone, and if the face is still growing, everything moves around it.

Too much growth hormone before puberty, while the long bones are still open, makes a person very tall, 7 feet or more. After puberty the long bones are fused, so they barely grow, and the condition is acromegaly. The hands and feet enlarge, but "look for the jaw in your patients": the mandible grows, so the bite changes, from a normal Class I to edge-to-edge or even a Class III malocclusion. The bigger arch leaves more room for the teeth, so diastemas open between them, and the tongue enlarges (macroglossia). Macroglossia also appears under hypothyroidism, so it is the jaw and the spacing that point to growth hormone.

Testosterone or DHT enters the cell and binds the androgen receptor (DHT is the main ligand, and testosterone binds it too), and the hormone-receptor complex changes gene expression. Because the effect goes through gene transcription, it takes time. Estradiol acts the same way through estrogen receptors.

Also flagged in class

  • Learn the examples in each class; the class name gives the mechanism, so know what each target enzyme or receptor does.
  • 5-alpha-reductase bioactivates testosterone to DHT, so its inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) lower androgen activity.
  • Hepatotoxicity is the testosterone side effect to know; liver disease is a contraindication.
  • Proscar and Propecia are both finasteride: the higher strength treats BPH, the lower strength hair loss.
  • Estrogens raise clotting factors 2, 7, 9 and 10, and the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors share the clot risk.
  • Tamoxifen is for ER-positive breast cancer only.
  • Know the red drugs: goserelin, finasteride, dutasteride, flutamide, bicalutamide, tamoxifen, raloxifene, anastrozole, progesterone, hydroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel, ulipristal.

You can skip

  • Of the androgen drugs, know testosterone and testosterone cypionate (the IM depot); the other analogs on his table were not his focus.
  • The rest of his second estrogen-effects slide (ACTH, well-being, binding globulins, FSH and LH inhibition) was skipped; know the clotting, lipid, bone, skin and uterine effects.
