What's tested
  • The white cells: "what you need to remember with white blood cells is we've got two classes and 5 types," the granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and the agranulocytes (monocytes, lymphocytes), with each one's share, look and job; and "platelets arise from megakaryocytes. That's just knowledge you should know"
  • B, T and NK cells: "when you hear the word humoral, think B-cell response"; the plasma cell ("associate that with antibody production and release"); helper (CD4) and cytotoxic (CD8) T cells, which read antigen on MHC; and NK cells, with no B or T markers, CD16 and ADCC, and his schematic of how MHC class I holds them back
  • Innate versus adaptive immunity, and what belongs to each
  • Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs: "the thymus and the bone marrow for our class" (GALT is not primary), "bone marrow, B cells, thymus, T cells," and the stroma: "epithelioreticular cells, you should associate that with the thymus"
  • The thymus (cortex and medulla, involution to fat, 95 to 99 percent of thymocytes selected out, the blood-thymus barrier, thymic education) and the lymph node (the sinuses the lymph runs through, and where B and T cells are activated, multiply and make antibody)
  • The spleen: "the main thing is just to really associate this PALS with the spleen," the T cell sheath around the central artery; the white and red pulp, the marginal zone and the splenic sinuses
  • What he said won't be asked: stained images ("I'm not gonna ask you any questions specifically on stained images") and the typical concentration of each cell

1 Recognizing the blood cells and their jobs: red cells (most of the cells) carry oxygen and carbon dioxide, platelets come from megakaryocytes ("just knowledge you should know") and start clotting, and the white cells come in two classes and five types: the granulocytes and the agranulocytes (monocytes and lymphocytes), each with its share, most to least common, its nucleus and its line in the hematopoiesis tree

Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Dr. Herr's guide to his own lecture, and it asks for general roles and basic organization. Recognize each blood cell and know its job: red cells carry oxygen and carbon dioxide, platelets (megakaryocyte fragments) start clotting, neutrophils kill bacteria, eosinophils fight parasites and allergy, basophils hold heparin, monocytes become macrophages. Then B cells (antibodies), T cells (CD4 helpers, CD8 killers) and NK cells; the bone marrow and thymus as primary organs versus the nodes, MALT and spleen as secondary; and the layout of the thymus (cortex, medulla), lymph node (B-cell follicles, T-cell paracortex) and spleen (white pulp with its PALS of T cells around the central arteriole, red pulp).
  • Platelets are pieces of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and they take part in clotting.

Hematology is the study of the blood and its cells. Blood holds three kinds of cells. The erythrocytes, the red blood cells, are most of them, about 99 percent of the cells in the blood, and they carry oxygen and carbon dioxide; oxygen transport is their main job. The platelets are pieces of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and they initiate blood clotting: he said they play a role in the clotting cascade. "Remember, platelets arise from megakaryocytes. That's just knowledge you should know." The rest are the white blood cells, or leukocytes, and "what you need to remember with white blood cells is we've got two classes and 5 types."

2 The white cells' jobs: the neutrophil (multi-lobed, about 10 hours in the blood, the first line of defense against bacteria), eosinophil (red granules, major basic protein against parasites, allergy), basophil (dark blue granules, heparin, asthma) and monocyte (becomes the macrophage and expresses MHC II)

Study guide + recording · 8 questions in the bank

Their granules hold two weapons. Peroxidase binds to microorganisms and helps kill them. Major basic protein, MBP, also called PRG2, binds to and disrupts the membranes of parasites, both protozoa and helminths (worms), and it also makes basophils release histamine.

Eosinophils and basophils both have a bilobed nucleus and IgE receptors. Tell them apart by the granules: red with eosin (the eosinophil: peroxidase and major basic protein, parasites and allergy) or dark blue to purple (the basophil: heparin and histamine, asthma).

3 B and T cells: B cells carry surface IgM and IgD, and a B cell whose antibody fits an antigen recruits helper T cells and becomes a plasma cell that releases that antibody, in a secondary organ; helper T cells (CD4, antigen on MHC II) help the B cells, cytotoxic T cells (CD8) kill what they bind, and T cells carry memory

Study guide + recording · 5 questions in the bank

Know this
  • A B cell whose antibody fits its antigen recruits helper T cells and becomes a plasma cell, which releases that antibody; in a lymph node, plasma cells secrete it in the medulla.

B lymphocytes carry the humoral response: "if you hear the word humoral, you're thinking B lymphocyte, you're thinking antibody production in some form or fashion." Each B cell makes and displays membrane-bound antibodies, IgM and IgD, which act as its receptors for antigens, and each mature B cell answers one antigen. His drawing showed it: a B cell whose antibody doesn't fit a star-shaped antigen can't bind it, but one whose antibody fits does. That binding generates a chemical signal that recruits helper T cells, and the B cell transforms into a plasma cell, which makes a great many antibodies like the one that bound and releases them into the circulation.

4 NK cells: the large lymphocytes, with no B or T markers and no specific receptors; MHC class I on a healthy cell binds the inhibitory receptor and stops the killing, a cell missing it is killed, and too many activating ligands cause induced killing; CD16 binds IgG's constant region in ADCC, with macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils

Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank

Know this
  • MHC class I on a healthy cell binds the NK cell's inhibitory receptor and stops the killing; a cell missing it is killed; far more activating ligands cause induced killing.

In ADCC, circulating antibodies bind the antigens on a target cell's surface. The Fc receptors on NK cells, macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils then bind the antibody-coated target, and the killer cell secretes lytic enzymes, perforins, TNF and granzymes (his slide's list), which together kill the target. The antibody picks the target and the killer cell does the killing, with no T cell receptor and no MHC involved. His ADCC picture puts a target cell in the middle with an NK cell, a neutrophil, an eosinophil and a macrophage around it: he had presented them one by one, but "they all play a role in concert together."

  • A healthy cell shows both the activating ligand and MHC class I. The activating receptor wants to bind the ligand, but the inhibitory receptor binds the MHC class I and stops that response: no killing.
  • A target cell, such as a tumor cell or a virus-infected cell, still has the activating ligand but is missing its MHC class I, the signal that says "cut it out." The activating receptor binds the ligand, and the NK cell kills the target.

5 Innate versus adaptive immunity: what the body just does (barriers, low pH, lysozyme, thiocyanate, interferons, phagocytes, NK cells), versus the antibodies of the humoral arm ("think B-cell response") and the T cells of the cellular arm

Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Humoral means B cells and antibodies; cellular means T cells, which target transformed cells.

Nonspecific, or innate, immunity is what "your body just does": pre-existing defenses against microbial invasion, in place without any sequence of events to set them off. It has five parts: physical barriers, the skin and mucous membranes; chemical defenses, such as the low pH of some regions of the body; secretory substances, such as lysozyme, thiocyanate (in saliva) and interferons; phagocytic cells, the macrophages, neutrophils and monocytes; and the natural killer (NK) cells.

Specific, or adaptive, immunity produces acquired resistance, and it takes a sequence of events. A first contact with a specific antigen starts a chain of reactions carried out by the effector B and T cells, and it often leaves a state of immune memory. It has two arms, which aren't independent: they act together. The humoral response belongs to the B cells: they make antibodies, which mark invaders for destruction by other cells. The cellular immune response belongs to the T cells: it targets transformed cells and virus-infected cells for destruction. His shortcut: "When you hear the word humoral, think B-cell response. And then also, when you hear B cells, think about the production of antibodies."

6 Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs: the primary ones are just the bone marrow and the thymus (not GALT), where B and T cells become immunocompetent without antigen ("bone marrow, B cells, thymus, T cells"; self-reactive B cells removed in the marrow); every other one, lymph nodes, MALT and GALT, and the spleen, is secondary

Study guide + recording · 5 questions in the bank

He narrowed the long list: "Really, what we want to remember is lymph nodes, MALT and GALT, and spleen. We'll look at the tonsils as well." The activation of B and T cells takes place in these peripheral, or secondary, organs: the cells originate in the primary organs, the self-reactive ones are removed, and the rest are sent out to be further educated and made into what they need to be. The secondary organs capture antigens and give lymphocytes a place to undergo clonal proliferation and differentiate into effector cells in the presence of those antigens. Each has its own job: the lymph nodes filter lymph; MALT and GALT, sitting with the epithelia, are the first defense against external antigens; and the spleen filters blood.

7 The spleen: the PALS, the T cell sheath around the central artery ("associate this PALS with the spleen"); the splenic artery from the celiac trunk bringing blood-borne antigens in, with no afferent lymphatics; white pulp and red pulp; the marginal zone; red pulp of cords and sinusoids; and what the spleen does

Study guide + recording · 8 questions in the bank

Know this
  • The PALS, the T cell sheath around the central artery of the white pulp, means the spleen: "if you see a central artery, that's where you have that area of PALS."

The spleen, a secondary lymphoid organ, filters blood and responds to systemic, blood-borne infections. It lies in the upper left quadrant of the abdomen, behind the stomach and just below the diaphragm. In adults it is the largest lymphoid organ, about the size of a clenched fist. At its hilum, the large splenic artery, a branch of the celiac trunk, enters with the nerves, and it carries the blood-borne antigens and lymphocytes into the spleen. The splenic vein and lymphatics leave there. It has no afferent lymphatics; its efferent lymphatics leave at the hilum.

The white pulp is islands of lymphoid tissue around a central arteriole (he called it the central artery), which comes from the splenic artery after many treelike branchings. In it he pointed out a primary follicle, a marginal zone, germinal centers and the PALS, the periarteriolar lymphatic sheath: the lymphocytes wrapped around the arteriole ("peri means around"), which "I'll just say is associated with the T-cell area." "The main thing is just to really associate this PALS with the spleen," he said, and at the end: "If you see a central artery, that's where you have that area of PALS." Lymphoid nodules lie farther out in the white pulp, and they are the B cells: primary nodules, or secondary ones with germinal centers, as in the lymph nodes. A nodule pushes the arteriole off to one side. Around the white pulp is a shell of sparsely cellular lymphoid tissue, the marginal zone, with macrophages and some B cells (his slide).

8 The thymus: epithelioreticular cells form its stroma ("I do want you to know that"), reticular cells and type III collagen everywhere else; the dense, dark cortex versus the lighter medulla; the blood-thymus barrier's three layers; and involution to fat by the teens

Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Every lymphoid organ's stroma is reticular cells and type III collagen except the thymus's, which is epithelioreticular cells.

Every lymphoid organ's cells sit in a stroma, an internal framework of cells, and the blood that flows into the organ passes through it, where it meets many cells and can set off many reactions. In every lymphoid organ except the thymus, the stroma is reticular cells and reticulin fibers, which are type III collagen. The thymus is the exception: its stroma is the cell processes of the epithelioreticular cells. "I do want you to know that. So epithelioreticular cells, you should associate that with the thymus."

It is very large when you are born and little: largest and most active in the newborn and before adolescence, about 12 to 15 grams at birth and 30 to 40 grams by puberty (his slide's numbers). By the time you are a teenager, or a little past then, it shrinks, which is thymic involution, and fat replaces it. He said that in a donor you see a lot of fat in front of the heart: that is where the old thymus was.

9 The lymph node: the lymph's route (afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, trabecular sinuses, efferent lymphatic); activation in the paracortex and follicles, B cells multiplying in germinal centers and plasma cells secreting antibody in the medulla; B cells in the follicles and T cells in the paracortex; dendritic and follicular dendritic cells; blood lymphocytes entering through high endothelial venules

Study guide + recording · 8 questions in the bank

His schematic follows the lymph. An afferent lymphatic vessel, with valves that direct the flow, brings lymph from the surrounding tissues into the subcapsular sinus, just under the capsule. From there it runs into the trabecular sinuses, beside the trabeculae, with the chance to pass through a germinal center on the way, and it leaves in the efferent lymphatic vessel. Around the sinuses are the outer cortex, with its superficial and deep layers, and the inner medulla, and blood comes into the node too, through its own capillaries. His slide adds how the filtering works: the sinus walls let the lymph percolate into the superficial and deep cortex, where the lymphocytes carry out immunosurveillance, and macrophages reach into the sinuses and phagocytose antigens and foreign material.

Lymphocytes also arrive from the blood. Blood comes in through an artery at the hilum, and its lymphocytes cross into the deep cortex through the high endothelial venules, HEVs. T cells and dendritic cells are directed to the paracortex, and B cells to the cortex. Both leave the node through the efferent lymphatic vessel. The lymph node is the only lymphoid structure with both afferent and efferent lymphatics.

10 T cell education: precursors in through postcapillary venules, out to the cortex, positive and negative selection, single CD4 or CD8 cells out to the secondary organs, and 95 to 99 percent selected out by apoptosis

Study guide + recording · 2 questions in the bank

Then come positive and negative selection, which most of the cells fail; his slide puts them in order. In the cortex, the epithelioreticular cells present antigen on MHC molecules: a thymocyte whose receptor recognizes them survives, and one that doesn't dies. This is positive selection. The survivors move into the medulla for negative selection, which eliminates the cells aimed at self antigen displayed on self MHC. The cells that pass both become CD8-positive cytotoxic or CD4-positive helper T cells, ready for an immune response, and they leave through postcapillary venules into the circulation and migrate to the secondary lymphoid organs.

11 The splenic sinuses and the blood's path: rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells with macrophage processes, strands of basal lamina at right angles, no smooth muscle and no pericytes; in the open circulation, sheathed capillaries empty into the cords

Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank

The splenic sinuses are special sinusoidal vessels. They are lined by rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells that run lengthwise, with slit-like spaces between them, and macrophage processes reach between the cells to monitor the passing blood for foreign antigens. They have only strands of basal lamina, which loop around the endothelial cells at right angles, like the hoops around the staves of a leaky barrel. They have no smooth muscle and no pericytes. Blood cells move across the wall by squeezing through the slits (his slide).

12 MALT and the tonsils: Peyer's patches in the ileum, under M cells that take microbes from the lumen; the pharyngeal, tubal (at the auditory tube), palatine and lingual tonsils, and the crypts that trap material; IgA into the lumen, and adenoiditis

Recording + objectives · 8 questions in the bank

  • the tubal tonsils, at the torus tubarius, where the auditory tube opens;

Together they form Waldeyer's ring, a broken circle of lymphoid tissue around the entrance to the nasopharynx and oropharynx. They sit where you breathe, eat and drink all day, so they start the response early: if you just ate a salmonella chicken sandwich, he said, it doesn't stop you from getting sick, but it starts to mount the response. The palatine tonsils have tonsillar crypts, where substances get wedged in, which gives the tissue a longer time to respond.

Also flagged in class

  • Granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) have prominent granules; agranulocytes (monocytes and lymphocytes) don't.
  • The primary lymphoid organs are just the bone marrow and the thymus; any other lymphoid organ, GALT included, is secondary.
  • B and NK cells form and mature in the marrow; T cell precursors leave it immunoincompetent and mature in the thymus.
  • In the thymus, 95 to 99 percent of thymocytes fail selection and die by apoptosis; macrophages clear them.

You can skip

  • Know each cell and region by its described features; no stained images on the exam ("there's not any images on your exam, necessarily").
  • Skip the counts per liter in his summary table; know each cell's name, share of the white count and job.
  • Skip the long list of lymphoid tissues on his overview figure; know which two are primary and what the main secondary ones do.
  • Skip the colony-forming unit names on the bone marrow slide (CFU-Ly, CFU-LyB, CFU-LyT); know what each blood cell line gives rise to.
  • Know the general roles: helper T cells help the B cells and cytotoxic T cells kill what they bind; he didn't go into how each one responds.
hy.lymleuk:
What's tested
  • The molecular associations he said you need ("you do need to know the molecular associations on the ones that are sort of underlined"): t(14;18) and BCL2 in follicular lymphoma, t(11;14) and cyclin D1 in mantle cell lymphoma ("if you got a test question, let's say this is expressing cyclin D1, you would know this is mantle cell lymphoma"), t(8;14) and MYC in Burkitt lymphoma, t(9;22) and the Philadelphia chromosome in CML, and t(15;17) and PML-RARA in acute promyelocytic leukemia
  • The categories ("I want you to know generally kind of what category things are"): which lymphomas are B-cell and which T-cell, which are indolent and which aggressive, acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid; and how Hodgkin lymphoma differs from non-Hodgkin lymphoma
  • Acute leukemia: blasts are the hallmark, and more than 20 percent blasts makes the diagnosis ("that's our threshold"), any count with a defining genetic abnormality; Auer rods mean a myeloid blast; AML in adults, ALL in young children; and the two acute leukemias "you need to know": acute promyelocytic leukemia (DIC, and an excellent cure with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide) and acute monocytic leukemia in the mouth
  • Chronic myeloid leukemia, "the main chronic leukemia that you need to know": the Philadelphia chromosome, every stage of maturation in the blood, imatinib; and CLL/SLL, one disease of small mature B cells with smudge cells
  • What a dentist sees: swollen gums from leukemia ("you guys may actually be the clue that a patient has leukemia"), bleeding gums, Burkitt lymphoma in the jaw, the palate destroyed by NK/T-cell lymphoma, and marginal zone lymphoma in the salivary glands ("the one you guys are going to experience the most"); and the B symptoms, "really high-yield clues" of lymphoma
  • What he said you don't need: the CD markers and the flow cytometry details ("don't waste your time learning that kind of stuff"), the AML subtypes, the differences between the classic Hodgkin subtypes, and the ALL details beyond who gets it

1 Classifying the leukemias on two axes: acute (blasts that don't mature) or chronic (cells that still mature), and myeloid or lymphoid: AML, ALL, CML and CLL

Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank

He came back to maturation when he turned to leukemia, calling it "one of the important concepts". The cells go through steps of maturation in the marrow as they acquire their function, and the neutrophil line, which his objectives ask for, shows it best: myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, and finally the segmented neutrophil, or PMN. The myeloblast is the youngest cell: very fine chromatin, prominent nucleoli and darker blue cytoplasm. In the promyelocyte the chromatin is still fine, the cytoplasm is less dark, and granules appear. In the myelocyte the chromatin turns clumped and coarse, the nucleus starts to indent, and the cytoplasm is less blue. In the band the nucleus is indented even more and the cytoplasm turns pink, and in the segmented neutrophil the nucleus is pinched into lobes. Only the neutrophils are released into the blood. (Aloud he went from the myelocyte straight to the band; his slide puts the metamyelocyte, with its kidney-shaped nucleus, between them.)

2 Acute versus chronic leukemia (onset, course, blasts, platelets, organomegaly) and leukemia's clinical consequences: marrow failure (anemia, bleeding, infection) and cells growing in tissues (bone pain, spleen, liver, nodes, and the gums, where a dentist may be the first clue)

  • Marrow failure, as the leukemic cells crowd out normal blood-making: anemia, with fatigue, malaise and pallor; bruising and bleeding from too few platelets; and fever and infections from too few working white cells.

Hodgkin lymphomaNon-Hodgkin lymphoma

He said the main Hodgkin lymphoma is classic Hodgkin lymphoma: "You don't need to know the non-classical." It is different from the rest. The tumor cells are a small fraction of the mass, sparse and very large, embedded in a reactive background rich in immune cells. They are the Hodgkin cells (one nucleus) and the Reed-Sternberg cells (two or more nuclei), together called HRS cells. The classic Reed-Sternberg cell has two nuclear lobes, each with a prominent, eosinophilic (pink) nucleolus, which gives it an owl's-eye look. "That's the main thing that you need to recognize, is those Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells." Stains such as CD30 and CD15 light them up, but the markers aren't needed.

4 AML's diagnostic threshold (more than 20 percent blasts; any count with a defining genetic abnormality), Auer rods (a myeloid blast, never ALL), AML in adults versus ALL in children, and the conditions acute leukemia can grow out of (myelodysplastic syndrome, CML)

Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Blasts are the hallmark of acute leukemia, and more than 20 percent, in the blood or the marrow, makes the diagnosis; an AML with a defining genetic abnormality needs no set count.

The number his objectives ask for is the blast threshold. He gave two ways to diagnose AML. With a specific cytogenetic abnormality, "you can diagnose AML right away. You don't even have to have 20% blasts." Without one, the blasts must be more than 20 percent, in the blood or the marrow: "That's our threshold for making the diagnosis." If the blood shows more than 20 percent, acute leukemia can be diagnosed from it; if it shows only a few, the marrow is examined. Fewer blasts than that, in a patient with abnormal counts, point to something else, such as a myelodysplastic syndrome (later in these notes).

  • Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS): persistent cytopenias with abnormal function and look of the red cell, granulocyte and/or megakaryocyte precursors. It may start with few blasts and progress to more.

5 ALL, the acute leukemia of young children (usually 1 to 5 years old, a poor prognosis under 1): B-ALL most often, and T-ALL, confirmed as T-cell by testing rather than by its look

Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank

Aloud he added a few points to the table below: AML is relatively rare in children; ALL is usually seen at 1 to 5 years of age, with a particularly poor prognosis under 1 year; AML's blasts have a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and may or may not hold Auer rods: "If you see Auer rods, that tells you that you're looking at a myeloid blast. Lymphoid blasts do not have Auer rods." The gonads, as a site outside the marrow, are more specific to ALL, and flow cytometry tells the two apart, by markers you don't need.

6 Chronic myeloid leukemia, the chronic leukemia he said to know: BCR-ABL1 and the Philadelphia chromosome, a very high count with every stage of maturation and few blasts, chronic versus blast phase, imatinib

Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank

Know this
  • CML: t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL1; a very high white count with every stage of maturation and few blasts; tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.

Its blood and marrow. The white count is high, from 12,000 to 1,000,000 per microliter, with a median of about 80,000 (the slide writes it as 12 to 1,000 times 10 to the 9th per liter). The cells are mostly neutrophils at every stage of maturation, with peaks at the myelocytes and the segmented neutrophils, not blasts. He put it as the full pattern of maturation, from early blasts all the way to neutrophils, all increased in the blood and the marrow, with a count high enough to separate it from a reactive one, such as an infection. The marrow is hypercellular, more than 95 percent cellular, with granulocytes at every stage, and his slide shows small, hypolobated megakaryocytes. The karyotype shows the Philadelphia chromosome.

Its treatment. Knowing the abnormal signal led to drugs that block it, the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, of which imatinib (Gleevec) was the first and is first-line therapy. It targets the enzymatically active part of the p210 BCR-ABL1 protein: it competes with ATP for the active site and so prevents the kinase from activating. He put it as blocking the binding site, so BCR-ABL1 can't bind its substrate and drive the cell to proliferate. In this era of kinase inhibitors, the most important sign of prognosis is the response to treatment, measured in the blood count, the chromosomes and the molecular test.

7 CLL/SLL: one disease of small, mature B cells, named by where it is (blood or node); soccer-ball chromatin and smudge cells; at least 5 times 10 to the 9th B cells per liter for CLL, below that monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis; older patients, infections, largely incurable

Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank

  • CLL is diagnosed from the blood: a B-cell count of at least 5 times 10 to the 9th per liter (5,000 per microliter), with the typical look and markers.

The look, which his objective stresses "particularly in blood": small lymphocytes with clumped chromatin, a pattern compared to cracked mud or a soccer ball, and many smudge cells, fragile lymphocytes that have burst apart as the smear is made. "That's a clue right away, I'm looking at that, I'm thinking CLL." The marrow can be involved in various patterns, which he said you don't need to know. In a lymph node the small cells infiltrate diffusely, with pale areas of larger cells called proliferation centers.

8 Burkitt lymphoma: very aggressive and very fast-growing, t(8;14) and MYC, the starry sky of macrophages eating debris, the jaw, EBV, and excellent survival with chemotherapy

Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Burkitt lymphoma's starry sky is macrophages eating the debris of tumor cells that proliferate very fast; it carries t(8;14), MYC with IGH.

Under the microscope: sheets of uniform, medium-sized, cohesive blue cells, with many tingible-body macrophages scattered among them. These macrophages have eaten the debris of tumor cells that died by apoptosis, and their pale cytoplasm against the dark blue sheet gives the classic starry-sky pattern, which he compared to Van Gogh's painting and called "the key morphologic finding in making this diagnosis". With modern immunochemotherapy including rituximab, in high-resource settings, the prognosis is excellent: overall survival over 90 percent in children and 80 percent in adults. He said that is why the diagnosis matters: the chemotherapy works.

9 Mantle cell lymphoma: from the follicle's mantle zone, t(11;14) (nothing else among the lymphomas carries it), the cyclin D1 stain, older adults with enlarged nodes, survival much longer than it was

Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Cyclin D1, switched on by t(11;14), means mantle cell lymphoma; he said nothing else among the lymphomas carries t(11;14).

Its genetic hallmark, and the first event in its development, is the translocation between chromosomes 11 and 14, t(11;14), present in at least 95 percent of cases. It switches on cyclin D1, and his slide calls the cyclin D1 stain diagnostic. He said the translocation "tells me right away, I'm looking at mantle cell lymphoma. Nothing else in the lymphomas will do that." Its cells carry CD5, like CLL/SLL's, so he needs another marker to tell them apart: cyclin D1, found by immunohistochemistry, not flow cytometry. "If you got a test question, let's say this is expressing cyclin D1, you would know this is mantle cell lymphoma."

10 Mycosis fungoides, the most common skin lymphoma, an indolent T-cell lymphoma (patches, then plaques, then tumors), and Sézary syndrome, its aggressive form (erythroderma, nodes and cerebriform Sézary cells in the blood)

He went through these quickly: "I'm not going to go over in much detail, but know that these are the most common types of cutaneous lymphomas that are involving the skin, and that they have an indolent course." Mycosis fungoides is a T-cell lymphoma of the skin; with Sézary syndrome it is the most common type of cutaneous lymphoma, more than half of cases. Its lesions evolve in sequence: patches, then plaques, then tumors. They can be one or many; when localized they favor sun-protected skin, the flexures (armpits and groin) and the lower trunk and buttocks, a "bathing-trunk" distribution. Under the microscope, small to medium-sized T cells with a clear halo and hyperchromatic, hyperconvoluted ("cerebriform") nuclei line up along the basal layer and infiltrate the epidermis: they are epidermotropic. The course is indolent, over years or decades, with lesions that persist and grow slowly. It can appear at any age, peaking in the late fifties.

Sézary syndrome is defined by a triad: erythroderma (red skin over most of the body), generalized lymphadenopathy, and clonal T cells with cerebriform nuclei, Sézary cells, in the skin, the lymph nodes and the peripheral blood. He called it the aggressive version, with the blood and the nodes involved; the cerebriform nuclei in the blood help confirm it, and the node involvement can be subtle. Unlike mycosis fungoides, it is aggressive: the 5-year survival is 10 to 30 percent, and most patients die of opportunistic infections.

  • Marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma: indolent, in the salivary glands and ocular adnexa, linked to H. pylori, Chlamydia psittaci, Sjögren syndrome and Hashimoto thyroiditis, with lymphoepithelial lesions as its key finding.

Most patients already have widespread disease when it is found: nodes both near the surface and deep in the chest and abdomen, and an enlarged spleen; the marrow is involved in 40 to 70 percent (he said fairly commonly), and occasionally the blood. Yet patients are often asymptomatic, and B symptoms are uncommon. It is indolent: the median survival is more than 17 years with current treatment. But it keeps progressing over time, with no plateau in the survival curves, and the prognosis is closely tied to how far it had spread at diagnosis.

12 The two acute leukemias he said you need: acute promyelocytic leukemia (t(15;17) PML-RARA, maturation stopped at the promyelocyte, DIC, cured by all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide) and acute monocytic leukemia, which can show in the gums

Know this
  • APL: t(15;17) fuses PML with RARA and stops maturation at the promyelocyte; know it for its DIC, which can kill, and for its excellent cure with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide.
  • Acute monocytic leukemia can show outside the marrow in the mouth, as swollen gums infiltrated by leukemic cells.

He named two acute leukemias "you need to know", and this is the first. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a type of AML in which abnormal promyelocytes predominate. Its genetic hallmark is a balanced translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17, t(15;17), which fuses the promyelocytic leukemia gene, PML, with the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene, RARA. The fusion protein, PML-RARA (written with a double colon on the slides), causes the disease by impairing myeloid differentiation: maturation stops at the promyelocyte.

Patients present with symptoms of their cytopenias, with disease outside the marrow, or both, and the oral cavity is one of those places. AML that forms a mass outside the marrow is called a myeloid sarcoma (extramedullary AML). In the mouth it shows as gingival hypertrophy: swollen gums infiltrated by leukemic cells. His slides cite two case reports, one of them a myeloid sarcoma of the mandibular gingiva that was the relapse of a treated AML. This is what his objective means by the extramedullary presentation of acute leukemia. He said a biopsy of those gums can look a little like lymphoma, but studies confirm the leukemia, and the marrow is diffusely full of blasts.

13 The other T- and NK-cell lymphomas: peripheral T-cell lymphoma (very aggressive, B symptoms, a poor response to chemotherapy) and extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (EBV, necrosis, a perforated palate)

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma is a lymphoma of NK-cell or T-cell lineage that damages and destroys blood vessels, with prominent necrosis, and a very strong association with EBV. It begins in the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx, Waldeyer ring or epiglottis. From the nose it can grow out into the face or erode the nasal floor, destroying and perforating the hard palate, the picture once called "lethal midline granuloma". A dentist may be the first to see it. He covered it briefly, as time ran short ("you guys may come across this"): EBV-associated lymphomas of the midline of the palate, perforating lesions from a very aggressive lymphoma causing necrosis.

15 Diagnosing lymphoma: the tissue makes the diagnosis (the B symptoms, high-yield clues, only raise the suspicion); an effaced node; flow cytometry shows the lineage and, with only kappa or only lambda, a clonal population; staging, with disseminated disease as stage 4

Recording + objectives · 5 questions in the bank

He set a normal lymph node beside a pathologic one. To the eye, a normal node is well circumscribed and rubbery; a lymphoma node is fleshy and plump, not circumscribed. Under the microscope a normal node has B-cell areas in its outer part, the cortex, with primary follicles and germinal centers, T-cell areas deeper in, and open (patent) sinuses between them, where the macrophages live and the lymphocytes pass in and out: patent sinuses are a clue that the node is benign. In a lymphoma the architecture is altered, or effaced: replaced by tumor cells, often one monotonous population. The lab reads the tissue three ways: the routine H and E stain for morphology; immunohistochemistry, antibodies that stain proteins in the section; and flow cytometry, which reads living cells one at a time in suspension. The H and E, purple and red, gives the baseline: normal or abnormal. If it looks abnormal, the extra studies ask whether it is a lymphoma and which one. Immunohistochemistry is an antibody to part of the cell that turns it brown: one stain lights up B cells, another looks for something abnormal on them.

His example of something abnormal: the light chains kappa and lambda. Each B cell carries only one of them, and a normal node has both, about 3 kappa to 1 lambda. A lymphoma's cells all come from one abnormal cell, so they show only kappa or only lambda: "that's a clue that I'm looking at something that's what we call clonal."

16 Plasma cell neoplasms: a solitary plasmacytoma versus multifocal myeloma in the marrow, rouleaux from the excess antibody, the M-spike, lytic bone, high calcium, kidney damage and anemia (CRAB)

He went through the findings: lytic bone lesions (punched-out holes in the bone on radiographs); an M-spike on protein electrophoresis, the monoclonal protein as one tall, narrow band; the CRAB features of organ damage, which stand for hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia and bone lesions; and rouleaux on the blood smear, red cells stacked like coins, because the large amount of immunoglobulin protein makes them stick together ("it makes this sticky"). Aloud he listed the clinical findings as hypercalcemia, renal impairment and anemia, with the lytic bone; the CRAB chart on his slide is a picture.

In the jaw, myeloma's lytic lesions are radiolucencies and its calcium is high, so it can look like the brown tumors of hyperparathyroidism from Lecture A. The monoclonal protein, the rouleaux and the anemia point to myeloma.

  • The B symptoms: a fever of 38 °C or higher, drenching night sweats that soak the sheets, and unexplained loss of at least 10 percent of body weight in 6 months; they raise the suspicion, and the tissue makes the diagnosis.
  • Swollen gums from leukemic cells growing in them can be the first sign of a leukemia nobody has found yet; with fatigue, pallor and bruising, get a blood count.

You can skip

  • Skip the individual CD markers; know that flow cytometry reads the surface antigens to tell B, T or myeloid, mature or blast, and something abnormal, such as a clone with only kappa or only lambda.
  • Skip the AML subtypes (M0 to M7) and the subtype lists of AML and ALL; know AML versus ALL, and the acute leukemias he named.
  • Skip the differences between the classic Hodgkin subtypes (and the non-classical type, which he also said you don't need); recognize the Reed-Sternberg cells.
  • Know only the gist he gave: a very aggressive T-cell lymphoma, usually with B symptoms, that doesn't necessarily respond to chemotherapy.
  • Mycosis fungoides: know that it is the most common lymphoma of the skin, a T-cell lymphoma with an indolent course, and that Sézary syndrome is its aggressive form, with the blood and nodes involved.
  • For B-ALL and T-ALL, know who gets them: mostly children (usually 1 to 5 years, poor prognosis under 1), less often adults; T-ALL is confirmed as T-cell by testing.
